Chapter 2: Noisy-label problems and datasets

Tasks, taxonomy, datasets, and evaluation

Abstract

This chapter starts with a definition of intrinsic label noise, followed by explanation of the main types of label noise, namely: symmetric, asymmetric, and instance-dependent noise. We also provide definitions of closed-set and open-set label noise problems. We then provide a detailed list of current datasets and benchmarks available in the field to assess label noise algorithms and models. The chapter is concluded with a presentation of the main evaluation methods used to assess the performance of approaches designed to address label noise problems.

Keywords

Intrinsic label noise; Symmetric label noise; Asymmetric label noise; Instance-dependent label noise; Open-set label noise; Noisy-label learning benchmark

2.1 Introduction

As explained in Fig. 1.5, there are four sources of label noise. To facilitate the formal definition of label noise in this chapter, we will cluster these four sources into two sources, namely: 1) the intrinsic noise associated with the difficulty of labeling the data (i.e., the insufficient information for reliable labeling, and the intrinsic variability among labelers from Fig. 1.5); and 2) the noise introduced by the labeler or by the encoding process (i.e., unreliable labeler and encoding/communication error from Fig. 1.5). It is important to consider these two noise clusters because the type and rate of label noise usually depends on both sources, as we will explain in this chapter. Fig. 2.1 shows a fictitious example3

In this chapter, we first define the regression, classification, segmentation, and detection problems assuming that data samples have an underlying intrinsic label distribution. Then, we explain the main types of label noise processes studied in the field, i.e., closed-set, open-set, symmetric, asymmetric, and instance-dependent, which are introduced by the labeling process. We then present the main datasets and benchmarks used to assess methods that are designed to address label noise problems, and we conclude the chapter with approaches to assess noisy-label classification, segmentation, and detection problems.

2.2 Regression, classification, segmentation, and detection problems

In this section, we provide a more formal description of the label noise learning problem, where we focus on regression, classification, segmentation, and detection problems.

2.2.1 Regression

For the regression problem, we have x ∈ 𝒳 denoting the input data sample (e.g., image, text, sound) and $\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} \in \mathcal{Y}$ representing the noisy label in a continuous space, which for regression problems is generally represented by 𝒴 ⊂ ℝ. Each training sample is drawn from a joint probability distribution defined by p(X, Ỹ) that is generally latent, unless we are dealing with toy problems where we can define such distribution. This probability distribution p(X, Ỹ) can be defined in the joint 𝒳 × 𝒴 space, where data x and noisy label $\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}$ are drawn simultaneously, but such joint distribution complicates the definition of label noise since the noise affecting the data is entangled with the noise affecting the label. Hence, we decompose p(X, Ỹ) into p(Ỹ|X)p(X) using the fundamental rule for probability calculus, which suggests a 2-stage sampling process, where we first draw x from p(X), and then a noisy label $\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}$ from p(Ỹ|X = x).

Without loss of generality, let us assume that both terms can be represented by normal distributions, so the joint probability distribution can be denoted as follows:

$p(X = \mathbf{x},\widetilde{Y} = \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = p(\widetilde{Y} = \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|X = \mathbf{x}) \times p(X = \mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{N}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}};\mu_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x}),\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x})) \times \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x};\mu,\Sigma),$

(2.1)

where

$\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x};\mu,\Sigma) = \frac{\exp\{ - \frac{1}{2}{(\mathbf{x} - \mu)}^{\top}\Sigma^{- 1}(\mathbf{x} - \mu)\}}{\sqrt{{(2\pi)}^{|\mathcal{X}|}|\Sigma|}}$

(2.2)

represents a multivariate normal distribution, with $\mathcal{N}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}};\mu_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x}),\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x}))$ being similarly defined, μ𝒳 : 𝒳 → 𝒴 denotes the function that returns the mean label in 𝒴 given x, Σ𝒳 : 𝒳 → 𝒴 × 𝒴 is the function that returns the label covariance in 𝒴 given x, and μ and Σ are the mean and covariance for the multivariate normal distribution in 𝒳. The sampling process then happens in two stages:

1. X = μ + Σ × ϵ𝒳2. Ỹ = μ𝒳(x) + Σ𝒳(x) × ϵ𝒴,

(2.3)

where ϵ𝒳 ∼ n(0𝒳, I𝒳) is a normally distributed pseudo-random vector in 𝒳 (with zero mean 0𝒳 ∈ 𝒳 and identity covariance I𝒳 ∈ 𝒳 × 𝒳), and similarly for ϵ𝒴 ∼ n(0𝒴, I𝒴) in 𝒴.

To introduce the concept of a latent clean label in regression problems, we consider another representation for the joint probability with p(X, Ỹ) = ∫p(Y, Ỹ|X)p(X)dY = ∫p(Ỹ|Y, X)p(Y|X)p(X)dY, where Y denotes the latent clean label variable. An example of this representation is:

$p(X = \mathbf{x},\widetilde{Y} = \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = \int p(\widetilde{Y} = \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|Y,X = \mathbf{x}) \times p(Y|X = \mathbf{x}) \times p(X = \mathbf{x})dY = \int\mathcal{N}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}};\mu_{\mathcal{YX}}(Y,\mathbf{x}),\Sigma_{\mathcal{YX}}(Y,\mathbf{x})) \times \mathcal{N}(Y;\mu_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x}),\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x})) \times \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x};\mu,\Sigma)dY,$

(2.4)

where μ𝒴𝒳 : 𝒴 × 𝒳 → 𝒴, Σ𝒴𝒳 : 𝒴 × 𝒳 → 𝒴 × 𝒴, and other definitions are as explained in (2.1). The sampling follows a 3-stage process:

1. X = μ + Σ × ϵ𝒳2. Y = μ𝒳(x) + Σ𝒳(x) × ϵ𝒴3. Ỹ = μ𝒴𝒳(y, x) + Σ𝒴𝒳(y, x) × ϵ𝒴,

(2.5)

where ϵ𝒳 ∼ n(0𝒳, I𝒳) and ϵ𝒴 ∼ n(0𝒴, I𝒴), following the same definitions as in (2.3).

In a regression problem, we define a model fθ : 𝒳 → 𝒴, parameterized by θ ∈ Θ, that is trained to produce the output in 𝒴 given an input in 𝒳. This training is based on an optimization that minimizes a loss function denoted by ℓ : 𝒴 × 𝒴 → ℝ, which is designed to penalize mistakes made by the model. Two examples of losses that are usually considered in regression problems are:

$\ell_{L1}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})) = {\|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} - f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\|}_{1},\text{~and~}\ell_{L2}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})) = \left\| \widetilde{\mathbf{y}} - f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \right\|_{2},$

(2.6)

which denote the L1 and L2 losses, respectively. The training of the regression model using the joint probability of sample X and noisy label Ỹ is then based on optimizing the model parameters that minimize the expectation of the loss function:

$\theta^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta \in \Theta}\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \sim p(X,\widetilde{Y})}\lbrack\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\rbrack.$

(2.7)

However, the optimization in (2.7) cannot be performed because in general the distribution p(X, Ỹ) is unknown. This issue is solved by optimizing a Monte-Carlo approximation of the expectation of the loss function (2.7), by averaging the loss on the training set containing noisy labels $\mathcal{D} = {\{{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}_{i}\}}_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}$, where $(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \sim p(X,\widetilde{Y})$. This optimization is referred to as empirical risk minimization (ERM), which is defined as:

$\theta^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta \in \Theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}}\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})).$

(2.8)

We show the results of two regression experiments, with one relying on the 2-step sampling process described in (2.3) (see Fig. 2.2), and the other based on the 3-step sampling process from (2.5) (see Fig. 2.3). Both approaches relied on a model fθ(.) that consists of a multi-layer perceptron (2 hidden layers, each with 10 nodes and Exponential Linear Unit (ELU) activation functions, and an output layer with a single linear output), which is trained with the ERM in (2.8) that minimizes the L2 loss in (2.6).

2.2.2 Classification

For the multi-class classification problem (see Fig. 2.4(a)), we assume to have input data x ∈ 𝒳 labeled with $\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} \in \mathcal{Y} = \{\mathbf{p}|\mathbf{p} \in {\{ 0,1\}}^{|\mathcal{Y}|}\text{,\ and~}\sum_{c = 1}^{|\mathcal{Y}|}\mathbf{p}(c) = 1\}$, which is a one-hot classification label, where the dimension |𝒴| denotes the number of classes. Compared to the regression problem, the main difference in the classification problem is that 𝒴 is a discrete (instead of continuous) space representing the presence or absence of the classes in the input data.

Similarly to the regression problem, for the multi-class classification problem, a more direct representation of the label noise is achieved from the decomposition p(X, Ỹ) = p(Ỹ|X)p(X). For example, we can have

$p(X = \mathbf{x},\widetilde{Y} = \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = p(\widetilde{Y} = \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|X = \mathbf{x}) \times p(X = \mathbf{x}) = p(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}};t_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x})) \times \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x};\mu,\Sigma),$

(2.9)

where t𝒳 : 𝒳 → Δ|𝒴| − 1 represents a function that outputs the categorical distribution at each x ∈ 𝒳, with $\Delta^{|\mathcal{Y}| - 1} = \{\mathbf{p}|\mathbf{p} \in {\lbrack 0,1\rbrack}^{|\mathcal{Y}|}\text{,\ and~}\sum_{c = 1}^{|\mathcal{Y}|}\mathbf{p}(c) = 1\}$ being the probability simplex (Boyd et al., 2004), $p(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}};t_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x})) = \prod_{c = 1}^{|\mathcal{Y}|}\mathbf{t}{(c)}^{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(c)}$ (with t = t𝒳(x)) (Bishop, 2006), and μ and Σ are the mean and covariance for the multivariate normal distribution in 𝒳. The sampling process is based on two stages:

1. X = μ + Σ × ϵ𝒳2. Ỹ = T𝒳 − 1(u; x),

(2.10)

where ϵ𝒳 ∼ n(0𝒳, I𝒳), following the definitions in (2.3), u ∼ 𝒰(0, 1) denotes a number in [0, 1] sampled from a uniform distribution, and T𝒳 − 1 : [0, 1] × 𝒳 → 𝒴 represents the inverse cumulative distribution function computed from t𝒳(x) (Olver and Townsend, 2013).

The clean label variable Y can be explicitly introduced into the formulation with p(X, Ỹ) = p(Ỹ|X)p(X) = ∑Yp(Y, Ỹ|X)p(X) = ∑Yp(Ỹ|Y, X)p(Y|X)p(X). In this representation, we also introduce the transition probability function that estimates the noisy categorical distribution of Ỹ given Y and X. An example of this representation is

$p(X = \mathbf{x},\widetilde{Y} = \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = \sum\limits_{\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{Y}}p(\widetilde{Y} = \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|Y = \mathbf{y},X = \mathbf{x}) \times p(Y = \mathbf{y}|X = \mathbf{x}) \times p(X = \mathbf{x}) = \sum\limits_{\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{Y}}p(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}};t_{\mathcal{Y}\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x})) \times p(\mathbf{y};t_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x})) \times \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x};\mu,\Sigma),$

(2.11)

where p(y; t𝒳(x)) and 𝒩(x; μ, Σ) are as defined in (2.9), and t𝒴𝒳 : 𝒴 × 𝒳 → Δ|𝒴| − 1 represents the transition probability function that outputs a categorical distribution for the label $\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}$ given y and x. The sampling process is based on three stages:

1. X = μ + Σ × ϵ𝒳2. Y = T𝒳 − 1(u; x)3. Ỹ = T𝒴𝒳 − 1(u; y, x),

(2.12)

where, as in (2.10), ϵ𝒳 ∼ n(0𝒳, I𝒳) and u ∼ 𝒰(0, 1), and T𝒳 − 1(.) and T𝒴𝒳 − 1(.) represent the inverse cumulative distribution functions computed from t𝒳(x) and t𝒴𝒳(y, x).

The classifier is defined as fθ : 𝒳 → Δ|𝒴| − 1, which is trained to output the probability for each class in 𝒴 given an input in 𝒳. This training process minimizes a loss function ℓ : 𝒴 × Δ|𝒴| − 1 → ℝ that penalizes misclassifications. Examples of losses that are usually considered in classification problems are:

ℓ01(y, fθ(x)) = δ(y ≠ OneHot(fθ(x))), ℓCE(y, fθ(x)) =  − y⊤log (fθ(x)), ℓBCE(y, fθ(x)) =  − y⊤log (fθ(x)) − (1 − y)⊤log (1 − fθ(x)), ℓHNG(y, fθ(x)) = max (0, 1 − y⊤fθ(x)), ℓNLL(y, fθ(x)) =  − log (fθ(y)(x)),

(2.13)

which are the 0-1 loss, the cross-entropy (CE) loss, the binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, the hinge loss, and the negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss, where OneHot : Δ|𝒴| − 1 → 𝒴 returns a binary vector with a ‘1’ in the class of maximum probability from fθ(x), and ‘0’ for all other classes, δ(.) denotes the indicator function, and fθ(y)(x) returns the output from the model fθ(x) for the class indexed by the one-hot vector (y). The training of the classifier to estimate the optimal parameter θ ∈ Θ using the joint probability of sample X and noisy label Ỹ is achieved by minimizing the loss function:

$\theta^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta \in \Theta}\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \sim p(X,\widetilde{Y})}\lbrack\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\rbrack,$

(2.14)

which is unfeasible since p(X, Ỹ) is unknown. This is mitigated by using the training set containing noisy labels $\mathcal{D} = {\{{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}_{i}\}}_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}$, where $(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \sim p(X,\widetilde{Y})$, to minimize the empirical risk with

$\theta^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta \in \Theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}}\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})).$

(2.15)

We show the results of two multi-class classification experiments, with one relying on the 2-step sampling process described in (2.10), and the other based on the 3-step sampling process from (2.12) (see Fig. 2.5). In both experiments, the 2-D data is generated by a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) using four components, with each component representing a separate class, where the class means are ( − 2,  − 2), ( − 2, 2), (2,  − 2), (2, 2), covariances are denoted by an identity matrix of size 2 × 2, and mixture weights are equal to 0.25. The two experiments use a model fθ(.) that consists of a multi-layer perceptron (1 hidden layer with 5 nodes and Exponential Linear Unit (ELU) activation functions, and an output layer with a softmax output), which is trained with ERM in (2.15) that minimizes the BCE loss in (2.13).

For multi-label classification problems (see Fig. 2.4(b)), the training samples x are annotated with $\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} \in \mathcal{Y} \subset {\{ 0,1\}}^{|\mathcal{Y}|}$, with $0 \leq \sum_{c = 1}^{|\mathcal{Y}|}\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(c) \leq |\mathcal{Y}|$, so each sample can be labeled with no classes or multiple classes. This modification from the multi-class classification scenario requires some changes in the definitions presented above.

First, the model needs to be redefined as fθ : 𝒳 → [0, 1]|𝒴|, which means that each label can have a separate probability of being present in the data. The noisy-label distribution also needs a redefinition with $p(\widetilde{Y} = \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|X = \mathbf{x}) = p(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|t_{\mathcal{X}}^{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{x}))$, where t𝒳𝒫 : 𝒳 → Δ2|𝒴| − 1 outputs a categorical distribution at each x ∈ 𝒳, with Δ2|𝒴| − 1 denoting the probability simplex for the label power set 𝒫. In this power set, each of the 2|𝒴| labels in 𝒫 denotes a different label combination from the classes in 𝒴 (Spolaôr et al., 2013). Following the idea above, we extend $p(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}};t_{\mathcal{X}}^{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{x})) = \prod_{c \in \mathcal{P}}\mathbf{t}^{\mathcal{P}}{(c)}^{\delta(\mathcal{P}(c) = \widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}$, with t𝒫 = t𝒳𝒫(x), δ(.) being the indicator function, and 𝒫(c) representing the cth element of the power set 𝒫.

For training the classification model, we could consider the same loss functions from (2.13) if we regard the problem as a multi-class problem, where the classes are the label combinations in the power set 𝒫. However, the size of this power set quickly becomes intractable, so in practice, multi-label problems use the BCE loss from (2.13) and the class-wise 0-1 loss defined by $\ell_{01 - ML}(\mathbf{y},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})) = \prod_{c = 1}^{|\mathcal{Y}|}\delta\left( \mathbf{y}(c) \neq \mathsf{Squash}\left( f_{\theta}^{(\mathbf{y}_{c})}(\mathbf{x}),\tau \right) \right)$, where y(c) ∈ {0, 1} represents the cth element of the label vector y, Squash : [0, 1] × [0, 1] → {0, 1}|𝒴| is a function that thresholds the cth output of the model to be either 0 or 1 per label (using a threshold τ ∈ [0, 1]), with this cth model output denoted by fθ(yc)(x). Training is similarly done by minimizing the empirical risk in (2.15).

2.2.3 Semantic segmentation

The semantic segmentation problem mainly applies to images, as shown in Fig. 2.4(c), where the input image is denoted by x ∈ 𝒳 ⊂ ℝH × W × R (with H= height, W= width, R= number of color channels), which is labeled by $\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} \in \mathcal{Y} \subset {\{ 0,1\}}^{H \times W \times C}$ (with C= being number of segmentation classes, and $\sum_{c = 1}^{C}\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(\omega,c) = 1$ for ω ∈ Ω indexing the image lattice of size H × W). The segmentation model, parameterized by θ ∈ Θ, is defined by fθ : 𝒳 → {Δω|𝒴| − 1}ω ∈ Ω, which outputs a pixel-wise categorical distribution for the image x ∈ 𝒳. The segmentation problem is an extension of the whole image classification problem from Section 2.2.2 to a pixel-wise classification. Hence all definitions in Section 2.2.2 can be extended to the segmentation problem, but with the modifications explained below.

The joint probability from (2.9) needs to redefine the categorical distribution function from t𝒳 : 𝒳 → Δ|𝒴| − 1 to tΩ𝒳 : 𝒳 → {Δω|𝒴| − 1}ω ∈ Ω, which represents a function that outputs a pixel-wise categorical distribution. Furthermore, we also redefine $p(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}};t_{\Omega\mathcal{X}}) = \prod_{\omega \in \Omega}\prod_{c = 1}^{|\mathcal{Y}|}\mathbf{t}{(\omega,c)}^{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(\omega,c)}$, where t(ω, c) denotes the probability of the cth class at the pixel ω computed from t = tΩ𝒳(x), $\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(\omega,c)$ represents the label of the cth class at ω, and it is assumed that the pixel-wise categorical distribution is independent within the image lattice Ω. The sampling process for the segmentation problem is similar to the one for classification in (2.10) with the same step 1, and step 2 performed in a pixel-wise manner with Ỹ(ω) = TΩ𝒳 − 1(u; x) for ω ∈ Ω and u ∼ 𝒰(0, 1), which is the inverse cumulative distribution function computed from tΩ𝒳(x). When introducing the latent clean label variable Y, the joint distribution p(X, Ỹ) from (2.11) needs to use tΩ𝒳𝒴 : 𝒴 × 𝒳 → {Δω|𝒴| − 1}ω ∈ Ω, where sampling in (2.12) is done with Ỹ(ω) = TΩ𝒳𝒴 − 1(u; y, x), which is the inverse cumulative distribution function computed from tΩ𝒳𝒴(y, x).

Another difference is in the definition of the loss functions, where the losses in (2.13) are now defined in a pixel-wise manner, but a global loss can also be considered, such as the Dice loss (Milletari et al., 2016):

$\ell_{Dice}(\mathbf{y},\widehat{\mathbf{y}}) = \frac{2\sum_{\omega \in \Omega}\mathbf{y}{(\omega)}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{y}}(\omega)}{\sum_{\omega \in \Omega}\mathbf{y}{(\omega)}^{\top}\mathbf{y}(\omega) + \sum_{\omega \in \Omega}\widehat{\mathbf{y}}{(\omega)}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{y}}(\omega)},$

(2.16)

where $\widehat{\mathbf{y}} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$. Segmentation problems are constrained to a single label per pixel, so we do not consider the multi-label classification for segmentation problems. Training with a noisy label dataset $\mathcal{D} = {\{{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}_{i}\}}_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}$ is usually done by minimizing a combination of a pixel-wise loss and a global loss, as with the ERM in:

$\theta^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta \in \Theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}}\left( \frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum\limits_{\omega \in \Omega}\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(\omega),\widehat{\mathbf{y}}(\omega)) \right) + \lambda \times \ell_{Dice}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\widehat{\mathbf{y}}),$

(2.17)

where $\widehat{\mathbf{y}} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$, and λ weights the contribution of the Dice loss.

2.2.4 Detection

To deal with the detection of visual objects from images (see Fig. 2.4(d)), we define the input image as x ∈ 𝒳 ⊂ ℝH × W × R (with H= height, W= width, R= number of color channels), which is associated with B bounding boxes, each represented by the top-left and bottom-right two-dimensional coordinates denoted by b ∈ ℬ ⊂ ℝ4 and labeled with the object class $\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} \in \mathcal{Y} \subset {\{ 0,1\}}^{|\mathcal{Y}|}$. The detection model, parameterized by θ ∈ Θ, is defined by fθ : 𝒳 → {Δa|𝒴| − 1×ℬa}a = 1A, where A is the fixed number of detections produced by the model. The detection problem can be seen as an extension of the image classification and regression problems, where we aim to regress a set of A bounding boxes of visual objects, together with their classification.

The joint distribution includes image, noisy bounding boxes, and labels, as follows:

$p(X = \mathbf{x},{\widetilde{Y}}_{1} = {\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{1},{\widetilde{B}}_{1} = {\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{1},...,{\widetilde{Y}}_{A} = {\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{A},{\widetilde{B}}_{A} = {\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{A}) = p({\widetilde{Y}}_{1} = {\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{1},{\widetilde{B}}_{1} = {\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{1},...,{\widetilde{Y}}_{A} = {\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{A},{\widetilde{B}}_{A} = {\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{A}|\mathbf{x}) \times p(X = \mathbf{x}) = \prod\limits_{a = 1}^{A}p({\widetilde{Y}}_{a} = {\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{a},{\widetilde{B}}_{a} = {\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{a}|X = \mathbf{x}) \times p(X = \mathbf{x}) = \prod\limits_{a = 1}^{A}p({\widetilde{Y}}_{a} = {\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{a}|{\widetilde{B}}_{a} = {\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{a},X = \mathbf{x}) \times p({\widetilde{B}}_{a} = {\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{a}|X = \mathbf{x}) \times p(X = \mathbf{x}) = \prod\limits_{a = 1}^{A}p({\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{a};t_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x}({\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{a}))) \times \mathcal{N}({\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{a};\mu_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathbf{x}),\Sigma_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathbf{x})) \times \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x};\mu,\Sigma),$

(2.18)

where the A bounding boxes are assumed to be independent from each other, $t_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x}({\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{a}))$ is the categorical distribution, defined in (2.9), at the image region inside the bounding box ${\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{a}$ (denoted by $\mathbf{x}({\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{a})$), $p({\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{a};t_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x}({\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{a})))$ is defined in (2.9), μℬ : 𝒳 → ℬ returns the bounding box mean in image x and Σℬ : 𝒳 → ℬ × ℬ returns the bounding box covariance for the multivariate normal distribution 𝒩(.), and 𝒩(x; μ, Σ) is defined in (2.1).

The sampling process for each bounding box happens in three stages:

$\text{1.~}X = \mu + \Sigma \times \epsilon_{\mathcal{X}}\text{2.~}\widetilde{B} = \mu_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathbf{x}) + \Sigma_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathbf{x}) \times \epsilon_{\mathcal{B}}\text{3.~}\widetilde{Y} = T_{\mathcal{X}}^{- 1}(u;\mathbf{x}(\widetilde{\mathbf{b}})),$

(2.19)

where ϵ𝒳 ∼ n(0𝒳, I𝒳) is defined as in (2.3), ϵℬ ∼ n(0ℬ, Iℬ) follow the definitions from (2.3), u ∼ 𝒰(0, 1) denotes a uniform random number in [0, 1], and T𝒳 − 1(.) is the inverse cumulative distribution from t𝒳, as defined in (2.10).

Similarly to the regression problem in Section 2.2.1 and the classification problem in Section 2.2.2, we can introduce the clean label variable Y and clean bounding box variable B. We then define the transition probability function that estimates the noisy bounding box given X with p(B̃|X) = ∫p(B, B̃|X)dB = ∫p(B̃|B, X)p(B|X)dB. We also need to define the transition probability function that estimates the noisy categorical distribution of Ỹ given Y, B̃, and X with p(Ỹ|B̃, X) = ∑Yp(Ỹ|Y, B̃, X)p(Y|B̃, X). Hence, we have

$p(\widetilde{Y} = \widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\widetilde{B} = \widetilde{\mathbf{b}}|X = \mathbf{x}) = \sum\limits_{\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{Y}}p(\widetilde{Y} = \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|Y = \mathbf{y},\widetilde{B} = \widetilde{\mathbf{b}},X = \mathbf{x}) \times p(Y = \mathbf{y}|\widetilde{B} = \widetilde{\mathbf{b}},X = \mathbf{x}) \times \ \ \ \ \ \ \int p(\widetilde{B} = \widetilde{\mathbf{b}}|B,X = \mathbf{x}) \times p(B|X = \mathbf{x})dB = \sum\limits_{\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{Y}}p(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}};t_{\mathcal{Y}\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x}(\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}))) \times p(\mathbf{y};t_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x}(\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}))) \times \ \ \ \ \ \ \int\mathcal{N}(\widetilde{\mathbf{b}};\mu_{\mathcal{BX}}(B,\mathbf{x}),\Sigma_{\mathcal{BX}}(B,\mathbf{x})) \times \mathcal{N}(B;\mu_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathbf{x}),\Sigma_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathbf{x}))dB,$

(2.20)

where we follow the same definitions as in (2.4) and (2.11).

The sampling process for each bounding box is based on five stages:

$\text{1.~}X = \mu + \Sigma \times \epsilon_{\mathcal{X}}\text{2.~}B = \mu_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathbf{x}) + \Sigma_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathbf{x}) \times \epsilon_{\mathcal{B}}\text{3.~}\widetilde{B} = \mu_{\mathcal{B}\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{b},\mathbf{x}) + \Sigma_{\mathcal{B}\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{b},\mathbf{x}) \times \epsilon_{\mathcal{B}\mathcal{X}}\text{4.~}Y = T_{\mathcal{X}}^{- 1}(u;\mathbf{x}(\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}))\text{5.~}\widetilde{Y} = T_{\mathcal{Y}\mathcal{X}}^{- 1}(u;\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x}(\widetilde{\mathbf{b}})),$

(2.21)

where we follow the definitions from (2.5), (2.12), and (2.19).

The detector is trained to minimize a combination of regression and classification loss functions using a noisy label dataset $\mathcal{D} = \left\{ (\mathbf{x}_{i},{\{{\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,j},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j}\}}_{j = 1}^{B_{i}}) \right\}_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}$, with the ERM defined as follows:

$\theta^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta \in \Theta}\frac{1}{A|\mathcal{D}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x}_{i},{\{{\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,j},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j}\}}_{j = 1}^{B_{i}}) \in \mathcal{D}}\ \sum\limits_{a = 1}^{A}\left( \ell_{C}(\mathbf{y}_{i,a}^{\ast},{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,a}) + \delta(\mathbf{y}_{i,a}^{\ast} \neq 0_{\mathcal{Y}}) \times \ell_{R}(\mathbf{b}_{i,a}^{\ast},{\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a}) \right),$

(2.22)

where ${\{{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,a},{\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a}\}}_{a = 1}^{A} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i})$, $\mathbf{b}_{i,a}^{\ast} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{b} \in {\{{\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,j}\}}_{j = 1}^{B_{i}}}\mathsf{IoU}(\mathbf{b},{\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a})$, with $\mathsf{IoU}(A,B) = \frac{|A\bigcap B|}{|A\bigcup B|}$ denoting the intersection over union operator and ${\{{\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,j}\}}_{j = 1}^{B_{i}}$ representing the noisy bounding box annotation. Also in (2.22), we have

$\mathbf{y}_{i,a}^{\ast} = \begin{cases} {{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j},} & {\text{if~}\mathsf{IoU}(\mathbf{b}_{i,a}^{\ast},{\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a}) > \tau} \\ {0_{\mathcal{Y}},} & \text{otherwise} \\ \end{cases},$

(2.23)

where each bounding box in ${\{{\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,j},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j}\}}_{j = 1}^{B_{i}}$ can be associated with only one detection in ${\{{\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a},{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,a}\}}_{j = 1}^{A}$, and 0𝒴 is a vector with zeros of size |𝒴|. In (2.22), the loss ℓC(.) is represented by one of the classification losses in (2.13), and the loss ℓR(.) is one of the regression losses in (2.6).

2.3 Label noise problems

Recall that the label noise discussed in Section 2.2 is represented by the joint probability distribution p(X, Ỹ), which can be decomposed in two ways, one depending on the intrinsic label distribution p(Ỹ|X), and the other relying on the latent transition distribution p(Ỹ|Y, X) and clean distribution p(Y|X). The intrinsic label noise for classification and regression problems is shown in Figs. 2.6 and 2.7. Also recall that label noise can be decomposed into two types, namely: an irreducible term that is associated with the difficulty of the annotation and therefore impossible to eliminate, and a labeling error introduced by human or semi-automated labelers. The algorithms presented in this book target to mitigate the second type of noise since the first type is in principle impossible to eliminate.

To define the label noise process made by labelers, we introduce the noise rate η ∈ [0, 1], and the noise type ν, which can be symmetric, asymmetric, and instance-dependent. To account for this noise, we need to re-define the joint probabilities from Section 2.2. First, let us re-define the decomposed joint probability by conditioning it on η and ν, as follows:

p(X, Ỹ|η, ν) = p(Ỹ|X, η, ν) × p(X) = ((1−η)×p(Ỹ|X)+η×p(Ỹ|X,ν)) × p(X),

(2.24)

where p(Ỹ|X) denotes latent conditional label distribution defined in (2.1) for regression problems and (2.9) for classification problems, and p(Ỹ|X, ν) represents the latent conditional noisy label distribution of type ν. By taking the transition distribution into account, the joint probability is re-defined as

$p(X,\widetilde{Y}|\eta,\nu) = \sum\limits_{Y \in \mathcal{Y}}p(\widetilde{Y}|Y,X,\nu,\eta) \times p(Y|X) \times p(X) = \sum\limits_{Y \in \mathcal{Y}}\left( (1 - \eta) \times p(\widetilde{Y}|Y,X) + \eta \times p(\widetilde{Y}|Y,X,\nu) \right) \times p(Y|X) \times p(X),$

(2.25)

where the latent transition probability p(Ỹ|Y, X) is as defined in (2.4) for regression and in (2.11) for classification, while p(Ỹ|Y, X, ν) represents the latent noisy transition distribution of type ν, and the sum is replaced by an integral for the regression problem of (2.4). This joint distribution can then be used to build the noisy training set with samples $(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \sim p(X,\widetilde{Y}|\eta,\nu)$.

The definitions in (2.24) and (2.25) are related to the definition of the label noise process explained in the first challenge presented in Section 1.3, which is related to definition of the label noise generation process that can be based on a label distribution (Thiel, 2008; Domingos, 2000) as in (2.24), or a label transition process (Pérez et al., 2007; Lawrence and Schölkopf, 2001) as in (2.25).

2.4 Closed set label noise problems

The defining property of closed-set label noise problems is that the hidden clean label of the data is always in the set (for classification) or range (for regression) of training labels 𝒴. Below we present closed-set label noise problems for classification and regression problems since both subsume the other applications (i.e., segmentation and detection).

2.4.1 Symmetric

In closed-set symmetric classification label noise, the noise is uniform and independent of the input data X and label Y, so this type of noise can be explained by encoding or communication errors, as mentioned in Section 1.2. Essentially, given a data sample X, with label distribution p(Ỹ|X), a symmetric label noise will mix a uniform distribution with the label distribution, so that the labeling process produces a noisy label that can produce an arbitrary random label. Fig. 2.8 shows an example of a training set with symmetric label noise in a classification problem, where it is clear that labels are corrupted in an uniform manner. Also, in Fig. 2.9, we see how a uniform label noise affects a regression problem, with an η rate of samples showing a uniform distribution of labels. This type of noise is defined by the latent conditional noisy label distribution of type ν = sym from (2.24), with

p(Ỹ|X, ν = sym) = 𝒰(𝒴),

(2.26)

where 𝒰(𝒴) represents a uniform distribution, where the probability for each label is $\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|}$. Similarly, if we are working with the latent transition distribution $p(Y|\overline{Y},X)$ as in (2.25), we define the latent noisy transition as

p(Ỹ|Y, X, ν = sym) = 𝒰(𝒴).

(2.27)

The closed-set symmetric regression label noise is similarly defined, but we need to establish a closed-set domain for the labels, which is in principle unbounded for regression problems. Therefore, we use a common definition of inlier from statistics (Wilcox, 2011) which defines that the closed set for the labels is 1.5× the interquartile range (IQR), where

IQR(p(Ỹ)) = Q3(p(Ỹ)) − Q1(p(Ỹ)),

(2.28)

with Q3(p(Ỹ)) being the upper quartile defined as the median of the second half of p(Ỹ), and Q1(p(Ỹ)) denoting the lower quartile defined as the median of the first half of p(Ỹ), and p(Ỹ) = ∫p(X, Ỹ)dX. For the purpose of defining regression label noise, we consider a low outlier value Ỹ for p(Ỹ) to be less than Q1(p(Ỹ)) − 1.5 × IQR(p(Ỹ)), and a high outlier to be more than Q3(p(Ỹ)) + 1.5 × IQR(p(Ỹ)). Hence, for closed-set symmetric regression label noise, the latent conditional noisy label distribution of (2.24) is defined by

p(Ỹ|X, ν = sym) = 𝒰(Q1(p(Ỹ))−1.5×IQR(p(Ỹ)),Q3(p(Ỹ))+1.5×IQR(p(Ỹ))),

(2.29)

where $\mathcal{U}(a,b) = \frac{1}{b - a}$ if Ỹ ∈ [a, b] and 0 otherwise. Similarly, if we are working with the latent transition distribution p(Ỹ|Y, X) as in (2.25), we define the latent noisy transition as

p(Ỹ|Y, X, ν = sym) = 𝒰(Q1(p(Ỹ))−1.5×IQR(p(Ỹ)),Q3(p(Ỹ))+1.5×IQR(p(Ỹ))).

(2.30)

2.4.2 Asymmetric

In closed-set asymmetric classification label noise, the label noise depends only on the true label denoted by Y, but not on the data X. In image classification, typical examples are the inherent ambiguity in classifying visual classes that are naturally similar, such as ‘wolf’ and ‘coyote’, or ‘crow’ and ‘raven’, as explained in Section 2.1. This noise type can happen due to unreliable labeling or the intrinsic variability among labelers. In this type of error, given the data X with label distribution p(Ỹ|X) and noisy label transition distribution p(Ỹ|Y, X), an asymmetric label noise will increase the probability of pre-defined pairwise label flippings. This type of noise can only be defined with the transition distribution and the latent conditional noisy label distribution of type ν = asym from (2.25), as follows

p(Ỹ|Y, X, ν = asym) = T,

(2.31)

where T ∈ [0, 1]|𝒴| × |𝒴| is a stochastic matrix with the label flipping probabilities

Ti, j = p(Ỹ = yi|Y = yj),

(2.32)

for yi, yj ∈ 𝒴 denoting the one-hot label with the ith and jth labels active, respectively. Fig. 2.10 shows an example of asymmetric label noise using the transition distribution depicted on the right-hand side of the image.

The closed-set asymmetric regression label noise can be similarly defined with the latent transition distribution in (2.25) as in:

p(Ỹ|Y, X, ν = asym) = p(Ỹ|Y),

(2.33)

where p(Ỹ|Y) is similarly defined as in (2.4), i.e.,

p(Ỹ|Y) = 𝒩(Ỹ; μ𝒴(Y), Σ𝒴(Y)),

(2.34)

where μ𝒴 : 𝒴 → 𝒴 and Σ𝒴 : 𝒴 → 𝒴 × 𝒴. Fig. 2.11 displays an asymmetric label noise regression problem with a simple p(Ỹ|Y) defined as a Gaussian with mean 2 × Y.

2.4.3 Instance-dependent

Instance dependent classification label noise consists of a noisy labeling process that depends on the data X and possibly on Y. Compared with the symmetric and asymmetric noise types above, instance-dependent noise is more realistic since the label noise distribution depends on the input data, taking into account that some instances are harder to label than other instances. This noise type can happen due to insufficient information in the data for a reliable labeling, unreliable labeling or the intrinsic variability among labelers. From (2.24), given an instance X, with label distribution p(Ỹ|X), instance-dependent noise (IDN) adds a noisy label distribution p(Ỹ|X, ν = idn), defined as:

p(Ỹ|X, ν = idn) = p(Ỹ; t𝒳idn(X)),

(2.35)

where t𝒳idn : 𝒳 → Δ|𝒴| − 1 is a function that returns a categorical noisy-label distribution for instance X. For the latent transition distribution p(Ỹ|Y, X) in (2.25), we define the latent noisy transition as

p(Ỹ|Y, X, ν = idn) = p(Ỹ; t𝒴𝒳(Y, X)) = T(X),

(2.36)

where t𝒴𝒳 : 𝒴 × 𝒳 → Δ|𝒴| − 1 is a function that returns a categorical noisy-label transition for instance X, and T ∈ [0, 1]|𝒴| × |𝒴| is a stochastic matrix with instance-dependent label flipping probabilities defined as

Ti, j(X) = p(Ỹ = yi|Y = yj, X),

(2.37)

for yi, yj ∈ 𝒴 denoting the one-hot vector with the ith and jth labels active, respectively. Fig. 2.12 shows an example of instance dependent label noise, where the IDN increases the chances of a sample to be corrupted by a symmetric label noise if it is closer to the origin.

The closed-set instance-dependent regression label noise is similarly defined using the label distribution p(Ỹ|X) from (2.24), given an instance X, as follows:

p(Ỹ|X, ν = idn) = 𝒩(Ỹ; μ𝒳(X), Σ𝒳(X)),

(2.38)

where μ𝒳 : 𝒳 → 𝒴 and Σ𝒳 : 𝒳 → 𝒴 × 𝒴. For the latent transition distribution p(Ỹ|Y, X) in (2.25), we define the latent noisy transition as

p(Ỹ|Y, X, ν = idn) = p(Ỹ; μ𝒴𝒳(Y, X), Σ𝒴𝒳(Y, X)),

(2.39)

where μ𝒴𝒳 : 𝒴 × 𝒳 → 𝒴 and Σ𝒴𝒳 : 𝒴 × 𝒳 → 𝒴 × 𝒴. Fig. 2.13 shows an instance-dependent label noise regression problem with μ𝒴𝒳(y, x) = 2 × y × x and Σ𝒴𝒳(y, x) = 1 in (2.39).

2.5 Open-set label noise problems

Open-set label noise problems are defined by having data instances whose clean labels are not in the set (for classification) or range (for regression) of training labels 𝒴. For classification problems containing open-set label noise, the training set contains samples from both the closed and open sets, where closed-set samples are defined by

$\mathcal{X}_{\eta}^{c} = \left\{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} \middle| \sum\limits_{\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{Y}}p(Y = \mathbf{y}|X = \mathbf{x}) = 1\text{~and~}\sum\limits_{\mathbf{y} \notin \mathcal{Y}}p(Y = \mathbf{y}|X = \mathbf{x}) = 0 \right\},$

(2.40)

where P(Y|X) is the latent distribution of clean labels, and open-set samples are defined by

$\mathcal{X}_{\eta}^{o} = \left\{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} \middle| \sum\limits_{\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{Y}}p(Y = \mathbf{y}|X = \mathbf{x}) = 0\text{~and~}\sum\limits_{\mathbf{y} \notin \mathcal{Y}}p(Y = \mathbf{y}|X = \mathbf{x}) = 1 \right\},$

(2.41)

with 𝒳 = 𝒳ηc⋃𝒳ηo and $\eta = \frac{|\mathcal{X}_{\eta}^{o}|}{|\mathcal{X}|}$.

For regression problems, the training set also contains samples from both the closed and open sets, where closed-set samples are defined by

𝒳ηc = {x∈𝒳|∫Y ∈ 𝒴p(Y|X=x)dY=1 and ∫Y ∉ 𝒴p(Y|X=x)dY=0},

(2.42)

where 𝒴 = 𝒰(Q1(p(Y)) − 1.5 × IQR(p(Y)), Q3(p(Y)) + 1.5 × IQR(p(Y))), with p(Y) = ∫p(X, Y)dX and Q1(p(Y)), IQR(p(Y)) and Q3(p(Y)) being defined in (2.29), and open-set samples are defined by

𝒳ηo = {x∈𝒳|∫Y ∈ 𝒴p(Y|X=x)dY=0 and ∫Y ∉ 𝒴p(Y|X=x)dY=1},

(2.43)

with 𝒳 = 𝒳ηc⋃𝒳ηo and $\eta = \frac{|\mathcal{X}_{\eta}^{o}|}{|\mathcal{X}|}$.

In open-set classification and regression noise, the noise rate η defines the proportion of samples belonging to the open set 𝒳ηo, so the latent conditional noisy label distribution from (2.24) is re-defined as

p(X, Ỹ|η, ν) = (δ(X∈𝒳ηc)×p(Ỹ|X)+δ(X∈𝒳ηo)×p(Ỹ|X,ν)) × p(X),

(2.44)

where η is as defined in (2.41), and δ(.) denotes an indicator function. Similarly, if we are working with the latent transition distribution p(Ỹ|Y, X) as in (2.25), we define the latent noisy transition as

$p(X,\widetilde{Y}|\eta,\nu) = p(X) \times \left( \delta(X \in \mathcal{X}_{\eta}^{c}) \times \sum\limits_{Y \in \mathcal{Y}}p(\widetilde{Y}|Y,X) \times p(Y|X) + \delta(X \in \mathcal{X}_{\eta}^{o}) \times \sum\limits_{Y \notin \mathcal{Y}}p(\widetilde{Y}|Y,X,\nu) \times p(Y|X) \right),$

(2.45)

where η is defined in (2.41), and δ(.) denotes the indicator function. For regression problem, the sums in (2.44) and (2.45) are replaced by integrals.

2.5.1 Open-set symmetric

The open-set symmetric classification label noise is uniform and independent of the input data X and clean label Y, where an open-set data sample in 𝒳ηo is labeled with any of the closed-set labels by sampling a uniform distribution (see Fig. 2.14, on the left). Considering the latent conditional noisy label distribution for the open set samples of type ν = symo from (2.44), we have

p(Ỹ|X, ν = symo) = 𝒰(𝒴),

(2.46)

where 𝒰(𝒴) is a uniform distribution with label probability equal to $\frac{1}{|\mathcal{U}|}$. When working with the latent transition distribution from (2.45), we have

p(Ỹ|Y, X, ν = symo) = 𝒰(𝒴).

(2.47)

For the open-set symmetric regression (see Fig. 2.14, on the right), the latent conditional noisy label distribution of (2.44) is defined by

p(Ỹ|X, ν = symo) = 𝒰(Q1(p(Ỹ))−1.5×IQR(p(Ỹ)),Q3(p(Ỹ))+1.5×IQR(p(Ỹ))),

(2.48)

where p(Ỹ) = ∫X ∈ 𝒳ηcp(X, Ỹ|η, ν)dX, IQR(p(Ỹ)) = Q3(p(Ỹ)) − Q1(p(Ỹ)), and $\mathcal{U}(a,b) = \frac{1}{b - a}$ if Ỹ ∈ [a, b] and 0 otherwise. With the latent transition distribution p(Ỹ|Y, X) from (2.45), we define the latent noisy label transition as

p(Ỹ|Y, X, ν = symo) = 𝒰(Q1(p(Ỹ))−1.5×IQR(p(Ỹ)),Q3(p(Ỹ))+1.5×IQR(p(Ỹ))),

(2.49)

where X ∈ 𝒳o.

2.5.2 Open-set asymmetric

Similarly to the closed-set asymmetric classification noise, the open-set asymmetric label noise depends only on the true label denoted by Y, as shown in Fig. 2.15, on the left. Asymmetric label noise will affect the latent conditional noisy label distribution of type ν = asymo from (2.44)

p(Ỹ|Y, X, ν = asymo) = T,

(2.50)

where T ∈ [0, 1]|𝒴| × |𝒴o| is a stochastic matrix with the label flipping probabilities between the labels inside and outside the set 𝒴, with the outside labels denoted by 𝒴o and

Ti, j = p(Ỹ = yi|Y = yj),

(2.51)

for yi ∈ 𝒴 and yj ∈ 𝒴o denoting the one-hot vectors with the ith and jth labels active, respectively.

The open-set asymmetric regression label noise can also be defined with the latent transition distribution in (2.24), as displayed on the right graph of Fig. 2.15, as in:

p(Ỹ|Y, X, ν = asymo) = p(Ỹ|Y),

(2.52)

where p(Ỹ|Y) can be defined as in (2.4), i.e.,

p(Ỹ|Y) = 𝒩(Ỹ; μ𝒴(Y), Σ𝒴(Y)),

(2.53)

where μ𝒴 : 𝒴o → 𝒴 and Σ𝒴 : 𝒴o → 𝒴 × 𝒴.

2.5.3 Open-set instance-dependent

Open-set instance dependent classification label noise consists of a noisy labeling process that depends on the data X and possibly on Y, as displayed on the left of Fig. 2.16. From (2.44), given an instance X, with label distribution p(Y|X), instance-dependent noise (IDN) adds a noisy label distribution p(Ỹ|X, ν = idno), defined as:

p(Ỹ|X, ν = idno) = p(Ỹ; t𝒳idno(X)),

(2.54)

where t𝒳idno : 𝒳ηo → Δ|𝒴| − 1 is a function that returns a categorical open-set noisy-label distribution for instance X. For the latent transition distribution p(Ỹ|Y, X) in (2.45), we define the latent noisy transition as

p(Ỹ|Y, X, ν = idno) = p(Ỹ; t𝒴𝒳idno(Y, X)) = T(X),

(2.55)

where t𝒴𝒳idno : 𝒴o × 𝒳ηo → Δ|𝒴| − 1 is a function that returns a categorical noisy-label distribution for instance X, and T(X) ∈ [0, 1]|𝒴| × |𝒴o| is a stochastic matrix with instance-dependent label flipping probabilities defined as

Ti, j(X) = p(Ỹ = yi|Y = yj, X),

(2.56)

for yi ∈ 𝒴 and yj ∈ 𝒴o denoting the one-hot vectors with the ith and jth labels active, respectively, and X ∈ 𝒳o.

The open-set instance-dependent regression label noise (see right of Fig. 2.16) is similarly defined using the label distribution p(Y|X) from (2.44), given an instance X, as follows:

p(Ỹ|X, ν = idno) = 𝒩(Ỹ; μ𝒳(X), Σ𝒳(X)),

(2.57)

where μ𝒳 : 𝒳ηo → 𝒴 and Σ𝒳 : 𝒳ηo → 𝒴 × 𝒴. For the latent transition distribution p(Ỹ|Y, X) in (2.45), we define the latent noisy transition as

p(Ỹ|Y, X, ν = idno) = p(Ỹ; μ𝒴𝒳(Y, X), Σ𝒴𝒳(Y, X)),

(2.58)

where μ𝒴𝒳 : 𝒴o × 𝒳ηo → 𝒴 and Σ𝒴𝒳 : 𝒴o × 𝒳ηo → 𝒴 × 𝒴.

2.6 Label noise problem setup

The label noise problems discussed in Sections 2.4 and 2.5 generally have a setup involving three datasets:

  • •  a training set $\mathcal{D} = {\{{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}_{i}\}}_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}$, where ${(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}_{i} \sim p(X,\widetilde{Y}|\eta,\nu)$, with unknown η > 0 and ν ∈ {sym, asym, idn, symo, asymo, idno};
  • •  a testing set that is formed with a noise rate η = 0 and represented by $\mathcal{T} = {\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i})\}}_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{T}|}$, where $(\mathbf{x}_{i},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i}) \sim p(X,\widetilde{Y})$; and
  • •  a validation set, with a noise rate η = 0, denoted by $\mathcal{V} = {\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i})\}}_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{V}|}$, where $(\mathbf{x}_{i},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i}) \sim p(X,\widetilde{Y})$.

Hence, the main challenge is on how to train a model using a noisy-label training set 𝒟 with unknown noise rate η and type ν, and to test the trained model with the testing set 𝒯 with η = 0. Some problems also rely on the validation set 𝒱, where |𝒱| <  < |𝒟|, that is formed with a noise rate η = 0 to facilitate the adaptation of the trained model to the testing set.

Another important point is that some problems may have a combination of E different noise types at different noise rates, so effectively, the joint distribution for these problems is denoted by p(X, Ỹ|{ηe, νe}e = 1E). When all noise types in {ηe, νe}e = 1E are closed-set label problems, the decomposed joint probability from (2.24) is re-defined as

$p(X,\widetilde{Y}|{\{\eta_{e},\nu_{e}\}}_{e = 1}^{E}) = p(\widetilde{Y}|X,{\{\eta_{e},\nu_{e}\}}_{e = 1}^{E}) \times p(X) = \left( \left( 1 - \sum\limits_{e = 1}^{E}\eta_{e} \right) \times p(\widetilde{Y}|X) + \sum\limits_{e = 1}^{E}\eta_{e} \times p(\widetilde{Y}|X,\nu_{e}) \right) \times p(X),$

(2.59)

and by taking the transition distribution into account, the joint probability is re-defined as

$p(X,\widetilde{Y}|{\{\eta_{e},\nu_{e}\}}_{e = 1}^{E}) = \sum\limits_{Y \in \mathcal{Y}}p(\widetilde{Y}|Y,X,{\{\eta_{e},\nu_{e}\}}_{e = 1}^{E}) \times p(Y|X) \times p(X) = \sum\limits_{Y \in \mathcal{Y}}\left( \left( 1 - \sum\limits_{e = 1}^{E}\eta_{e} \right) \times p(\widetilde{Y}|Y,X) + \sum\limits_{e = 1}^{E}\eta_{e} \times p(\widetilde{Y}|Y,X,\nu_{e}) \right) \times p(Y|X) \times p(X).$

(2.60)

When all noise types in {ηe, νe}e = 1E are open-set label noise problems, the latent conditional noisy label distribution from (2.44) is re-defined as

$p(X,\widetilde{Y}|{\{\eta_{e},\nu_{e}\}}_{e = 1}^{E}) = \left( \delta(X \in \mathcal{X}_{\sum\eta_{e}}^{c}) \times p(\widetilde{Y}|X) + \sum\limits_{e = 1}^{E}\delta(X \in \mathcal{X}_{\eta_{e}}^{o}) \times p(\widetilde{Y}|X,\nu_{e}) \right) \times p(X),$

(2.61)

where $\sum\eta_{e} = \frac{\sum_{e = 1}^{E}|\mathcal{X}_{\eta_{e}}^{o}|}{|\mathcal{X}|}$ represents the sum of all E noise rates, so this means that the proportion of closed-set samples 𝒳∑ηec ∈ 𝒳 is $\left( 1 - \sum_{e = 1}^{E}\eta_{e} \right)$. When working with the latent transition distribution p(Ỹ|Y, X) as in (2.45), we define the latent noisy transition as

$p(X,\widetilde{Y}|{\{\eta_{e},\nu_{e}\}}_{e = 1}^{E}) = p(X) \times \left( \delta(X \in \mathcal{X}_{\sum\eta_{e}}^{c}) \times \sum\limits_{Y \in \mathcal{Y}}p(\widetilde{Y}|Y,X) \times p(Y|X) + \sum\limits_{e = 1}^{E}\delta(X \in \mathcal{X}_{\eta_{e}}^{o}) \times \sum\limits_{Y \notin \mathcal{Y}}p(\widetilde{Y}|Y,X,\nu_{e}) \times p(Y|X) \right).$

(2.62)

We can also have a combination of closed-set and open-set label noise. Let us represent the closed-set noise set with {ηe, νe}e = 1E and the open-set noise with {ηeo, νeo}e = 1Eo, then the latent conditional noisy label distribution is defined as

$p(X,\widetilde{Y}|{\{\eta_{e},\nu_{e}\}}_{e = 1}^{E},{\{\eta_{e}^{o},\nu_{e}^{o}\}}_{e = 1}^{E^{o}}) = \left( \delta(X \in \mathcal{X}_{\sum\eta_{e}^{o}}^{c}) \times \left( \left( 1 - \sum\limits_{e = 1}^{E}\eta_{e} \right) \times p(\widetilde{Y}|X) + \sum\limits_{e = 1}^{E}\eta_{e} \times p(\widetilde{Y}|X,\nu_{e}) \right) + \sum\limits_{e = 1}^{E^{o}}\delta(X \in \mathcal{X}_{\eta_{e}^{o}}^{o}) \times p(\widetilde{Y}|X,\nu_{e}^{o}) \right) \times p(X),$

(2.63)

and the latent noisy transition as

$p(X,\widetilde{Y}|{\{\eta_{e},\nu_{e}\}}_{e = 1}^{E},{\{\eta_{e}^{o},\nu_{e}^{o}\}}_{e = 1}^{E^{o}}) = p(X) \times \left( \delta(X \in \mathcal{X}_{\sum\eta_{e}^{o}}^{c}) \times \sum\limits_{Y \in \mathcal{Y}}\left( \left( 1 - \sum\limits_{e = 1}^{E}\eta_{e} \right) \times p(\widetilde{Y}|Y,X) + \sum\limits_{e = 1}^{E}\eta_{e} \times p(\widetilde{Y}|Y,X,\nu_{e}) \right) \times p(Y|X) + \sum\limits_{e = 1}^{E^{o}}\delta(X \in \mathcal{X}_{\eta_{e}^{o}}^{o}) \times \sum\limits_{Y \notin \mathcal{Y}}p(\widetilde{Y}|Y,X,\nu_{e}^{o}) \times p(Y|X) \right).$

(2.64)

The second and fifth challenges from Section 1.3 are related to the setup of the problem. In particular, the second challenge is about the experimental setup of the problem, where the datasets, noise rate, and noise type can lead to a combinatorial explosion in the number of benchmarks, which can hinder progress given the impossibility of assessing all proposed models on all benchmarks. Another point highlighted in the second challenge is the possible presence of label noise in the testing and validation sets. This issue can happen in real-world datasets since it may not be possible to acquire clean-label testing and validation sets. For instance, the diagnosis of certain conditions from medical images can be challenging, leading to high-level of label noise due the uncertainty of the diagnosis, making it impossible to have a clean label, unless we use a different source of information for the labels, such as pathology or surgery. The fifth challenge is about the estimation of the label noise rate and type present in a dataset, which is hard to obtain, but can be useful during the training process (Xiao et al., 2015; Liu and Tao, 2015). Frénay and Verleysen (2014) introduced a generic way to use such noise estimation information with a graphical model to explain closed-set symmetric, asymmetric, and instance-dependent noise, where a binary random variable represents the presence of error in the labeling process.

2.7 Datasets and benchmarks

In this section, we introduce the main datasets and benchmarks used to assess noisy label learning methods. We present the amount of training, validation, and testing images present in each dataset and benchmark, the estimated proportion and type of noise present, and the task (e.g., classification, segmentation, detection, etc.) used in the assessment. We divided the datasets into Computer Vision Datasets, Medical Image Analysis Datasets, and Non-image Datasets.

2.7.1 Computer vision datasets and benchmarks

Let us first introduce the datasets that contain approximately 0% of intrinsic label noise in the training, validation, and testing sets. MNIST (LeCun, 1998)4

Tiny-ImageNet (Karpathy et al., 2016)5

While the datasets above have negligible amount of noise, the next datasets were collected in such a way that they naturally contain label noise introduced by the labeling process in the training set, but the validation and testing sets still contains approximately 0% of intrinsic label noise. Animal-10N (Song et al., 2019)6

The CIFAR-10N, CIFAR-100N (Wei et al., 2021a)7

Food-101N (Lee et al., 2018)8

The dataset Clothing1M (Xiao et al., 2015)9

WebVision (Li et al., 2017)10

For the assessment of noisy-label methods for segmentation and detection problems, the main datasets used are Cityscapes (Cordts et al., 2016), COCO (Lin et al., 2014), PASCAL VOC (Everingham et al., 2010), and Potsdam+Vaihingen (Potsdam, 2018; Vaihingen, 2018). The Cityscapes (Cordts et al., 2016)11

2.7.1.1 Classification benchmarks

The real-world classification benchmarks are represented by the datasets Animal-10N (Song et al., 2019), CIFAR-10N, CIFAR-100N (Wei et al., 2021a), Food-101N (Lee et al., 2018), Clothing1M (Xiao et al., 2015), and WebVision (Li et al., 2017). These datasets contain specific types and rates of label noise, and methods are compared by verifying their classification accuracy on their clean testing sets. Even though useful, the real-world noisy label datasets above have fixed label noise rates and types, which do not allow for a systematic evaluation of the methods. To address this issue, many benchmarks have been proposed, where different types and rates of label noise are artificially introduced to the clean label datasets from Table 2.1 (i.e., all datasets that have noise rate η ≈ 0). Such artificially built benchmarks enable a systematic assessment of the methods with respect to label noise.

For the asymmetric label noise in CIFAR-10, Tanaka et al. (2018); Patrini et al. (2017) proposed the following four pairs of label transitions to be used in the transition matrix described in Section 2.4.2: TRUCK → AUTOMOBILE, BIRD → AIRPLANE, DEER → HORSE, CAT ↔ DOG. These transitions are parameterized by η ∈ [0, 1], where the probability of the ground truth (in the diagonal of the transition matrix) and noisy-label transition are η − 1 and η, respectively. The asymmetric label noise for CIFAR-100 (Karim et al., 2022) relies on a transition matrix that contains label flippings for each class to the next one within the super-classes (note that the 100 classes in the CIFAR-100 are grouped into 20 super-classes).

2.8 Evaluation

Noisy-label learning methods are assessed using many of the measures already used in the field to test regular classification, segmentation, and detection methods, but using the noise rate η as an independent variable, when it is available. When η is not available or fixed at a specific value, e.g., for real-world datasets, then comparisons are done with pre-defined training and testing sets. For the evaluations described below, the training is performed with a training set containing noisy labels $\mathcal{D} = {\{{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}_{i}\}}_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}$, with noise rate η > 0, while the evaluation measure is computed using the clean testing set denoted by $\mathcal{T} = {\{{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}_{i}\}}_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{T}|}$, which as explained in Section 2.6, is formed with a noise rate η = 0. Below, we list the most common measures to assess multi-class and multi-label classification, segmentation, and detection approaches.

2.8.1 Classification evaluation

For multi-class classification problems (see Fig. 2.17), the most common measure is the accuracy in the testing set, computed from:

$\mathsf{Accuracy} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{T}}{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{y}},$

(2.65)

where the test image label produced by the model is represented by $\widehat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathsf{OneHot}(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))$, with fθ : 𝒳 → Δ|𝒴| − 1 being the trained model and OneHot : Δ|𝒴| − 1 → 𝒴 denoting a function to produce a one-hot prediction from the model (2.13). Accuracy represents a sample-wise measure that works well when the number of samples per class in the testing set 𝒯 is balanced. However, when the number of samples per class is imbalanced, accuracy can provide a result that is biased toward the classes that contain the majority of samples. For instance, assume that we have a binary classification problem with 90 samples for class 1 and 10 samples for class 2, and the model predicts the correct class for all 90 samples of class 1, but predicts the correct class for only 5 samples of class 2, so even though the accuracy from (2.65) is 95%, the accuracy for class 2 is only 50%. Hence, in problems where we have highly imbalanced distributions of samples per class, the label-wise measures that we explain below are preferred.

A common label-wise measure is the area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUROC), which is displayed in Fig. 2.17. To compute this curve, we need to compute the following the true positive rate (TPR, also known as recall or sensitivity) and the false positive rate (FPR or 1-specificity) per class c ∈ {1, ..., |𝒴|} at several classification thresholds τ ∈ [0, 1],

$\mathsf{TPR}(c,\tau) = \frac{\mathsf{TP}(c,\tau)}{\mathsf{TP}(c,\tau) + \mathsf{FN}(c,\tau)}\mathsf{FPR}(c,\tau) = \frac{\mathsf{FP}(c,\tau)}{\mathsf{TN}(c,\tau) + \mathsf{FP}(c,\tau)},$

(2.66)

with

$\mathsf{TP}(c,\tau) = \sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{T}}\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(c) \times \delta(f_{\theta}^{(\mathbf{y}_{c})}(\mathbf{x}) \geq \tau),\mathsf{FN}(c,\tau) = \sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{T}}\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(c) \times \delta(f_{\theta}^{(\mathbf{y}_{c})}(\mathbf{x}) < \tau),\mathsf{FP}(c,\tau) = \sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{T}}(1 - \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(c)) \times \delta(f_{\theta}^{(\mathbf{y}_{c})}(\mathbf{x}) \geq \tau),\mathsf{TN}(c,\tau) = \sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{T}}(1 - \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(c)) \times \delta(f_{\theta}^{(\mathbf{y}_{c})}(\mathbf{x}) < \tau),$

(2.67)

where δ(.) is an indicator function, and fθ(yc)(x) represents the probability of classification for the cth class. The ROC curve per class c is computed by interpolating the values of TPR(c, τ) as a function of FPR(c, τ) by varying the threshold τ from 1 to 0. The AUROC for c is then computed as the area under the ROC curve for the class c, and the result for all classes is computed from the mean of the AUROC for all classes.

Another common label-wise measure used in classification problems is the area under the precision and recall curve (AUPRC), shown in Fig. 2.17, and the mean average precision (mAP). Both measures need the plotting of the precision-recall curve, where Recall(c, τ) = TPR(c, τ) in (2.66), and

$\mathsf{Precision}(c,\tau) = \frac{\mathsf{TP}(c,\tau)}{\mathsf{TP}(c,\tau) + \mathsf{FP}(c,\tau)},$

(2.68)

where TP(.), FP(.) are defined in (2.67). The PR curve is then computed by interpolating the values of Precision(c, τ) as a function of Recall(c, τ) by varying the threshold τ from 1 to 0. Even though PR and ROC curves are equivalent, PR curves are preferred for datasets that show highly imbalanced label distributions (Davis and Goadrich, 2006). From the PR curves, there are two label-wise measures that are usually computed to summarize the performance of methods. The AUPRC is the area under the PR curve, while the mAP is calculated from the average precision (AP), estimated as the weighted sum of precision values, where recall increases, as follows:

$\mathsf{AP}(c) = \sum\limits_{t = 1}^{|\mathcal{R}| - 1}\left( \mathsf{Recall}(c,\tau(t)) - \mathsf{Recall}(c,\tau(t + 1)) \right) \times \mathsf{Precision}(c,\tau(t)),$

(2.69)

where ℛ denotes the set of threshold values where recall increases, τ(t) is the threshold at position t in ℛ, Recall(c, τ(|ℛ|)) = 0, and Precision(c, τ(|ℛ|)) = 1. The mAP is then computed as the mean of the AP(c) over the classes c ∈ {1, ..., |𝒴|}.

Multi-label classification problems are generally evaluated with AUROC, mAP, and AUPRC since these measures can be computed in a class-wise manner and then summarized over the classes. Nevertheless, other measures have also been used by noisy-label multi-label learning approaches (Xie and Huang, 2021), such as the following (Zhang and Zhou, 2013):

$\mathsf{HammingLoss}(\tau) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}| \times |\mathcal{Y}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{T}}\sum\limits_{c \in \{ 1,...,|\mathcal{Y}|\}}\delta\left( \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(c) \neq {\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{\tau}(c) \right),\mathsf{OneError} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{T}}\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(\arg\max\limits_{c \in \{ 1,...,|\mathcal{Y}|\}}f_{\theta}^{(\mathbf{y}_{c})}(\mathbf{x})) = 0,\mathsf{Coverage} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{T}}\max\limits_{c:{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i}(c) = 1}\mathsf{rank}(f_{\theta}^{(\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{c}})}(\mathbf{x})) - 1,\mathsf{RankLoss} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{T}}\frac{1}{\#(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} = 1) \times \#(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} = 0)}|\mathcal{K}(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}),\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})|,$

(2.70)

where ${\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i}^{\tau} = \mathsf{Squash}(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}),\tau)$ with the Squash(.) defined in Section 2.2.2 as a function that thresholds the output using δ(fθ(x) > τ), rank(fθ(yc)(x)) returns the rank of the label c according to the classification confidence fθ(yc)(x), $\#(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} = 1)$ is a function that returns the number of labels in $\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}$ annotated with “1”, $\#(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} = 0)$ returns the number of labels annotated with “0”, and $\mathcal{K}(f_{\theta}^{(\mathbf{y}_{c})}(\mathbf{x}),\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = \{(c^{\prime},c^{''})|f_{\theta}^{(\mathbf{y}_{c^{\prime}})}(\mathbf{x}) < f_{\theta}^{(\mathbf{y}_{c^{''}})}(\mathbf{x}),\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(c^{\prime}) = 1,\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(c^{''}) = 0\}$ is the set of mis-ranked labels.

2.8.2 Segmentation evaluation

The evaluation of noisy-label segmentation methods can in principle be done with pixel-wise accuracy, using the formula in (2.65). However, segmentation problems tend to present extremely imbalanced distributions of classes, so accuracy is not well suited. A particularly interesting measure that is robust to such imbalanced distributions is the intersection over union (IoU), or also known as the Jaccard index. Recall that the pixel-wise segmentation label is denoted by $\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(\omega,c) \in \{ 0,1\}$ where ω ∈ Ω and c ∈ {1, ..., |𝒴|}, and the segmentation model produces a pixel-wise classification $\widehat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathsf{OneHot}(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))$, where $\widehat{\mathbf{y}}(\omega,c) \in \{ 0,1\}$. The IoU is computed for each image and class c as follows (see Fig. 2.18):

$\mathsf{IoU}({\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{c}) = \frac{{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{c}\bigcap{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{c}}{{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{c}\bigcup{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{c}} = \frac{\mathsf{TP}({\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{c})}{\mathsf{TP}({\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{c}) + \mathsf{FP}({\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{c}) + \mathsf{FN}({\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{c})},$

(2.71)

where ${\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{c}$ denotes the cth channel of the segmentation map $\widehat{\mathbf{y}}$ (similarly for ${\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{c}$), and

$\mathsf{TP}({\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{c}) = \sum\limits_{\omega \in \Omega}\widehat{\mathbf{y}}(\omega,c) \times \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(\omega,c),\mathsf{FP}({\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{c}) = \sum\limits_{\omega \in \Omega}\widehat{\mathbf{y}}(\omega,c) \times (1 - \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(\omega,c)),\mathsf{FN}({\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{c}) = \sum\limits_{\omega \in \Omega}(1 - \widehat{\mathbf{y}}(\omega,c)) \times \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(\omega,c).$

(2.72)

In (2.71), elements that have division by zero are generally ignored. Then, the mean IoU (mIoU) is computed with

$\mathsf{mIoU} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}| \times |\mathcal{Y}|}\sum\limits_{c \in \{ 1,...,|\mathcal{Y}|\}}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{T}}\mathsf{IoU}({\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{c}).$

(2.73)

Another measure commonly used to assess semantic segmentation methods is the Dice measure, computed for each image and class c as

$\mathsf{Dice}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\widehat{\mathbf{y}},c) = \frac{2 \times \mathsf{IoU}({\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{c})}{1 + \mathsf{IoU}({\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{c})},$

(2.74)

and the mean Dice over testing images and classes provides the final measure for the method. Dice and IoU allow similar interpretation of methods, but notice that Dice is larger than IoU, particularly when IoU is small, when Dice is two times larger.

In segmentation problems, it is possible that we have a set of labels per image (Zhang et al., 2020a) and that the method also produces a set of predictions per image, allowing us to estimate a distribution of labels instead of a single binary mask per class. The measure used for such cases is the class-wise generalized energy distance (GED) (Székely and Rizzo, 2013; Salimans et al., 2018; Bellemare et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020a), computed as

$D_{GED}^{2}\left( p(\widetilde{Y}|X = \mathbf{x}),p(\widehat{Y}|X = \mathbf{x}),c \right) = 2 \times \mathbb{E}\left\lbrack d(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\widehat{\mathbf{y}},c) \right\rbrack - \mathbb{E}\left\lbrack d(\widehat{\mathbf{y}},{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{\prime},c) \right\rbrack - \mathbb{E}\left\lbrack d(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{\prime},c) \right\rbrack,$

(2.75)

where $\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{\prime} \sim p(\widetilde{Y}|X = \mathbf{x})$ denote samples from the ground truth annotation distribution, $\widehat{\mathbf{y}},{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{\prime} \sim p(\widehat{Y}|X = \mathbf{x}) = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i})$ represent samples from the distribution learned by the trained model, and $d(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\widehat{\mathbf{y}},c) = 1 - \mathsf{IoU}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\widehat{\mathbf{y}},c)$ is a distance measure. Then, by averaging DGED2(p(Ỹ|X=xi),p(Ŷ|X=xi),c) over the classes, we obtain the GED measure for the method.

2.8.3 Detection evaluation

The evaluation of detectors depends not only on the correct localization of the visual object, but also on the classification of the detected region. Recall from Section 2.2.4 that the detection testing set is denoted by $\mathcal{T} = \left\{ \mathbf{x}_{i},{\{{\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,j},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j}\}}_{j = 1}^{B_{i}} \right\}_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{T}|}$, and the model outputs ${\{{\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a},{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,a}\}}_{a = 1}^{A} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i})$, where ${\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,j},{\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a} \in \mathbb{R}^{4}$, ${\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j} \in {\{ 0,1\}}^{|\mathcal{Y}|}$, and ${\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,a} \in \Delta^{|\mathcal{Y}| - 1}$. Detection methods are usually evaluated with mAP, but with the following re-definitions of precision and recall:

$\mathsf{Precision}(c,\tau,\tau_{IoU}) = \frac{\mathsf{TP}(c,\tau,\tau_{IoU})}{\mathsf{TP}(c,\tau,\tau_{IoU}) + \mathsf{FP}(c,\tau,\tau_{IoU})},\mathsf{Recall}(c,\tau,\tau_{IoU}) = \frac{\mathsf{TP}(c,\tau,\tau_{IoU})}{\mathsf{TP}(c,\tau,\tau_{IoU}) + \mathsf{FN}(c,\tau,\tau_{IoU})},$

(2.76)

where

$\mathsf{TP}(c,\tau,\tau_{IoU}) = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{B_{i}}{\mathsf{TP}\_\mathsf{Detection}}({\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,j}^{c},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j}^{c},{\{{\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a}^{c},{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,a}^{c}\}}_{a = 1}^{A},\tau,\tau_{IoU}),\mathsf{FP}(c,\tau,\tau_{IoU}) = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum\limits_{a = 1}^{A}{\mathsf{FP}\_\mathsf{Detection}}({\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a}^{c},{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,a}^{c},{\{{\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,j}^{c},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j}^{c}\}}_{j = 1}^{B_{i}},\tau,\tau_{IoU}),\mathsf{FN}(c,\tau,\tau_{IoU}) = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{B_{i}}{\mathsf{FN}\_\mathsf{Detection}}({\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,j}^{c},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j}^{c},{\{{\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a}^{c},{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,a}^{c}\}}_{a = 1}^{A},\tau,\tau_{IoU}).$

(2.77)

In (2.77), we have

  • •  ${\mathsf{TP}\_\mathsf{Detection}}({\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,j}^{c},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j}^{c},{\{{\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a}^{c},{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,a}^{c}\}}_{a = 1}^{A},\tau,\tau_{IoU})$ first checks if ${\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j}^{c} = 1$, then if at least one of the detections in ${\{{\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a}^{c},{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,a}^{c}\}}_{a = 1}^{A}$ has $\mathsf{IoU}({\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,j}^{c},{\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a}^{c}) > \tau_{IoU}$ and ${\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,a}^{c} \geq \tau$, then returns “1”; otherwise returns “0”;
  • •  ${\mathsf{FP}\_\mathsf{Detection}}({\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a}^{c},{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,a}^{c},{\{{\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,j}^{c},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j}^{c}\}}_{j = 1}^{B_{i}},\tau,\tau_{IoU})$ first checks if ${\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,a}^{c} \geq \tau$, then if all annotations in ${\{{\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,j}^{c},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j}^{c}\}}_{j = 1}^{B_{i}}$ have ${\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j}^{c} = 0$ or ${\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j}^{c} = 1$ and $\mathsf{IoU}({\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,j}^{c},{\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a}^{c}) < \tau_{IoU}$, then returns “1”; otherwise returns “0”;
  • •  ${\mathsf{FN}\_\mathsf{Detection}}({\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,j}^{c},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j}^{c},{\{{\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a}^{c},{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,a}^{c}\}}_{a = 1}^{A},\tau,\tau_{IoU})$ first check if ${\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j}^{c} = 1$, then if all detections in ${\{{\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a}^{c},{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,a}^{c}\}}_{a = 1}^{A}$ have ${\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,a}^{c} < \tau$ or ${\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,a}^{c} \geq \tau$ and $\mathsf{IoU}({\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,j}^{c},{\widehat{\mathbf{b}}}_{i,a}^{c}) < \tau_{IoU}$, then returns “1”; otherwise returns “0”.

Given the precision and recall computed from (2.76), we can compute AP(c) per class as from (2.69), and then the mAP as the mean of AP(c) over all classes at a particular IoU threshold τIoU. Fig. 2.19 shows examples of TP_Detection, FP_Detection, and FN_Detection for the detection of people from images.

2.9 Conclusion

In this chapter, we presented the formal definition of the different types of label noise for classification, regression, segmentation, and detection problems. We then presented the datasets and benchmarks relevant for the study of label noise, followed by an explanation of the main methods used to assess the performance of methods designed to address label noise problems. Next, we focus on theoretical aspects of noisy-label learning, then on noisy-label learning techniques and proposed methods.
