The aleatoric uncertainty $\mathbf{p}_{m} = \mathbb{E}_{q_{\lambda}(\theta)}\left\lbrack \mathbb{V}_{p(Y|X,\theta)}\left\lbrack \widetilde{\mathbf{y}} \right\rbrack \right\rbrack$ is then trained to approximate the multi-grader variability $\mathbf{p}_{g} = \mathbb{V}_{p(\mathcal{D})}\lbrack\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}\rbrack$ with

$\ell_{al} = - \frac{\gamma}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x}_{i},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i}) \in \mathcal{D}}\left\lbrack \mathbf{p}_{g}\log\mathbf{p}_{m} + (1 - \mathbf{p}_{g})\log(1 - \mathbf{p}_{m}) \right\rbrack.$

(4.87)

A relatively different approach from the ones above is the Classifier Refinement Of croWD-sourced LABels (CROWDLAB) (Goh et al., 2022) that takes a trained classifier and estimates a consensus label (with a confidence score) per training sample, and a rating for each annotator to assess the correctness of their labels. CROWDLAB relies on a weighted ensemble of classifier predictions, where weights are estimated based on the trustworthiness of each annotator relative to the given classifier. After training a model fθ : 𝒳 → Δ|𝒴| − 1 using consensus labels derived from majority voting using $\mathcal{D} = {\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},{\{{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j}\}}_{j = 1}^{M})\}}_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}$, they first score the consensus label quality with:

$f_{\theta_{CR}}^{(\widehat{\mathbf{y}})}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{w \times f_{\theta}^{(\widehat{\mathbf{y}})}(\mathbf{x}) + \sum_{j = 1}^{M}w_{j} \times f_{\theta_{j}}^{(\widehat{\mathbf{y}})}(\mathbf{x})}{w + \sum_{j = 1}^{M}w_{j}},$

(4.88)

where $\widehat{\mathbf{y}}$ denotes the consensus label, $f_{\theta}^{(\widehat{\mathbf{y}})}(\mathbf{x})$ represents the trained model prediction for class $\widehat{\mathbf{y}}$,

$f_{\theta_{j}}^{(\widehat{\mathbf{y}})}(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} {P,} & {\text{~if~}{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{j} = \widehat{\mathbf{y}}} \\ {\frac{1 - P}{|\mathcal{Y}| - 1},} & \text{~otherwise} \\ \end{cases}$

(4.89)

is the annotator-specific model prediction, with $P = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j = 1}^{M}\delta({\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i,j} = {\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i})$ (δ(.) is the indicator function), and the trustworthiness weights w and {wj}j = 1M represent the ensemble weights of the model and annotators, respectively, that are in general computed as 1 minus the estimated relative error of the trained model and annotator-specific models (Goh et al., 2022). Furthermore, CROWDLAB also ranks the annotators using the score {aj}j = 1M, with aj ∈ [0, 1] computed with the weighted average of the label quality score and the annotator agreement with consensus labels (Goh et al., 2022). Armed with the consensus labels, their confidence score, and the annotator ratings, it is then possible to eliminate the labels produced by low-ranked annotators and request the re-labeling of low-confidence labels.

Multi-rater learning is a fertile and relatively unexplored research topic, with applications in noisy-label learning and uncertainty estimation. The main issue with these approaches is the cost associated with the collection of multiple labels per image. Techniques that can generate new labels per image from its estimated label distribution (Nguyen et al., 2023) can mitigate this labeling cost problem if they can reliably substitute human labeling. The next years should witness an increasing investigation of multi-rater learning for noisy-label learning.

4.3.5 Prior knowledge

Prior information can be helpful when handling noisy-label learning, particularly when the information can constrain the optimization process. An interesting prior information about noisy-label learning is studied in (Seo et al., 2019) that explores the idea that by transforming the original problem containing |𝒴| classes into another problem where subsets of these classes are merged to form |𝒞| < |𝒴| meta-classes, we reduce the noise rate in the training set (see Fig. 4.22). Consider that the original noise rate is provided by

$\eta(\mathcal{D}) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}}\delta(\mathbf{y} \neq \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}),$

(4.90)

where y is the hidden true label of x, and δ(.) is the indicator function. Also assume that the new set of meta classes 𝒞m merged a few of the classes from 𝒟 to form a new training set 𝒟m, so the new noise rate is

$\eta(\mathcal{D}^{m}) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}^{m}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{c}}) \in \mathcal{D}^{m}}\delta(\mathbf{c}^{m} \neq {\widetilde{\mathbf{c}}}^{m}),$

(4.91)

where cim and ${\widetilde{\mathbf{c}}}_{i}^{m}$ are the hidden true and visible noisy meta class for xi in 𝒟m. It is trivial to show that η(𝒟m) < η(𝒟) (Seo et al., 2019). For instance, let us say that two samples xi and xj belong to the same class (i.e., yi = yj), but the label for xj has been corrupted, which means that ${\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i} \neq {\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{j}$. By merging ${\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i}$ and ${\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{j}$ into the same meta class, we have ${\widetilde{\mathbf{c}}}_{i}^{m} = {\widetilde{\mathbf{c}}}_{j}^{m}$, i.e., the two samples share the same clean label again. Seo et al. (2019) propose the implementation of {𝒟m}m = 1M meta-class sets and the training of M separate classifiers {fθm : 𝒳 → 𝒞m}m = 1M for those training sets. Inference is performed with

$p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\prod_{m = 1}^{M}f_{\theta^{m}}^{\mathsf{meta}(\mathbf{y},m)}(\mathbf{x})}{\sum_{\widehat{\mathbf{y}} \in \mathcal{Y}}\prod_{m = 1}^{M}f_{\theta^{m}}^{\mathsf{meta}(\widehat{\mathbf{y}},m)}(\mathbf{x})},$

(4.92)

where meta(y, m) outputs the meta class from the mth set of meta classes that contains the label y. The meta classes should be formed by merging the original classes that have common properties, which can be achieved by applying the k-means clustering algorithm. The prior information above is always true, but to properly explore this idea, one may need to have a large number of meta-class sets, with the inconvenience of needing to train one classifier per meta-class set.

A widely adopted noisy-label learning technique is the one that aims to estimate the noise transition matrix from clean-label to noisy-label learning, which will be explained in more detail in Section 4.5.1. The reliability of this estimation process requires clean-label samples or a large training set. An alternative based on a prior knowledge provided by humans is proposed in (Han et al., 2018b), where the idea is to constrain the optimization with a transition matrix mask that eliminates the possibility of estimating invalid class transition probabilities (e.g., images of beach cannot be confused with images of mountain), as shown in Fig. 4.23. In general, the optimization involving a transition matrix is formulated by

$\theta^{\ast},\mathbf{T} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta,\mathbf{T}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}}\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{T}^{\top}f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\text{s.t.~}\mathbf{T} \in {\lbrack 0,1\rbrack}^{|\mathcal{Y}| \times |\mathcal{Y}|}$

(4.93)

where T represents the noisy-label transition matrix. In principle, this can be solved by adding an explicit structure constraint s(T) = S0, with s(.) extracting T's matrix structure S0 ∈ {0, 1}|𝒴| × |𝒴|. However, as pointed out in (Han et al., 2018b), such training strategy has a few issues, such as: 1) it is unclear which distance measure to use to compute the distance between the learned transition matrix T and the prior S0; and 2) the complexity of training (4.93) for large-scale problems using Lagrange multipliers. Han et al. (2018b) proposed the use of variational learning to maximize the following evidence lower bound (ELBO) that approximates the log-likelihood of the noisy data, as follows

$\log p(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{x}) \geq \mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{T})}\left\lbrack \log\sum\limits_{\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{Y}}p(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{y},\mathbf{T})p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}) - \log\left( q(\mathbf{S}_{0})/p(\mathbf{S}_{0}) \right)|_{\mathbf{S}_{0} = s(\mathbf{T})} \right\rbrack,$

(4.94)

where q(T) represents the variational distribution to approximate the posterior of the noise transition matrix T, $q(\mathbf{S}_{0}) = q(\mathbf{T})\frac{d\mathbf{T}}{d\mathbf{S}_{0}}|_{\mathbf{S}_{0} = s(\mathbf{T})}$, and p(S0) is the structure prior.

Another possible prior knowledge to explore in noisy-label learning is the fact that models with simpler hypothesis and smoother decision boundaries are less prone to overfit to the noisy-label samples, and consequently generalize better (Luo et al., 2019). The low dimensionality of the deep representation subspace of training samples is a way to represent such simpler hypothesis and smoother decision boundaries (Ma et al., 2018). The dimensionality can be measured with the Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID) of the underlying data subspace/submanifold (Houle, 2017). In practice, the LID of the deep representation z from a data point x can be estimated as follows (Levina and Bickel, 2004; Amsaleg et al., 2015):

$\widehat{\mathsf{LID}}(\mathbf{z}) = - \left( \frac{1}{K}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{K}\log\frac{r_{i}(\mathbf{z})}{r_{\max}\left( \mathbf{z} \right)} \right)^{- 1}$

(4.95)

where ri(z) represents the distance between z and its ith nearest neighbor, and rmax(z) is the maximum distance to all the K nearest neighbors from z. In general, noisy-label learning has a LID compression in the early training stages, followed by a LID expansion in later training stages (Fig. 4.24 shows LID values for clean and noisy-label samples). On the contrary, when labels are clean, LID reduces continuously until the last training stages. Ma et al. (2018) proposed a training optimization with:

$\theta_{t}^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}}\ell\left( \alpha_{t} \times \widetilde{\mathbf{y}} + (1 - \alpha_{t}) \times f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}),f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \right)$

(4.96)

where t indexes the training epoch, and

$\alpha_{t} = \exp\left( - (t/T)\frac{{\widehat{\mathsf{LID}}}_{t}}{\min_{j = 0}^{t - 1}{\widehat{\mathsf{LID}}}_{j}} \right),$

(4.97)

with ${\widehat{\mathsf{LID}}}_{t} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}\widehat{\mathsf{LID}}(\mathbf{z}_{i})$ denotes the mean LID score at training epoch t ∈ {1, ..., T}. Hence, this optimization is a simulated annealing algorithm that finds a balance between LID and prediction performance. In particular, at the LID compression stage (early training epochs), αt → 1 and training relies on the training labels. At the LID expansion stage (i.e., overfitting phase at later training epochs), αt → 0, favoring model prediction. Fig. 4.25 shows a comparison between a training using the LID prior from (4.96) and a regular training with CE loss without any regularization. Notice that the probability map from the LID training looks closer to the clean-label map, and the LID values tend to go down during training, differently from the LID values from the CE loss training.

Exploring prior data knowledge is a strategy that can lead to strong results. However, discovering sensible priors to explore is a challenging task that requires good knowledge of the problem and creativity. Furthermore, some priors may be specific to particular applications and do not generalize well to all possible applications. The optimization using priors can also introduce operational challenges, such as with the optimization presented in (Han et al., 2018b).

4.3.6 Data augmentation

Data augmentation (Shorten and Khoshgoftaar, 2019; Cubuk et al., 2019, 2020; DeVries and Taylor, 2017; Hendrycks et al., 2019) is a method to generate new training samples from the original ones in the training set with the goal of increasing the diversity and size of the training set to regularize training and improve generalization. For images, this generation is based on applying relatively small transformations to the original training samples using several techniques, such as cropping, rotation, flipping, scaling, or image noise addition. The selection of data augmentation functions is a challenging task that can be automated (Cubuk et al., 2019, 2020) for specific datasets and learning tasks.

In noisy-label learning, data augmentation has been used mostly as a regularization technique (Song et al., 2022). For image-based problems, data augmentation usually relies on the traditional techniques of cropping, rotation, flipping, etc. However, Nishi et al. (2021) introduced the Augmented Descent (AugDesc) technique into noisy-label learning. AugDesc relies on two sets of data augmentation strategies: a weak augmentation based on traditional techniques of cropping, rotation, flipping, etc.; and a strong augmentation based on automated data augmentation selection methods (Cubuk et al., 2019, 2020) (see Fig. 4.26). Then, AugDesc uses the weak augmentation for sample selection and re-labeling, and the strong augmentation for the back-propagation step. The optimization of AugDesc is as follows (see Fig. 4.27):

$\theta^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}}\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \mathcal{A}_{S}}\left\lbrack \mathsf{clean}(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \times \ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(a(\mathbf{x})) + (1 - \mathsf{clean}(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})) \times \ell(\widehat{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(a(\mathbf{x})) \right\rbrack$

(4.98)

where

$\widehat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \mathcal{A}_{W}}\left\lbrack f_{\theta}(a(\mathbf{x}) \right\rbrack,$

(4.99)

with 𝒜S and 𝒜W representing the sets of strong and weak augmentation functions a : 𝒳 → 𝒳, and clean : 𝒳 × 𝒴 → {0, 1} being a function that classifies a training sample into clean (returns 1) or noisy (returns 0). We show an example of the optimization from (4.98) in Fig. 4.28. A similar idea has been explored in (Smart and Carneiro, 2023), where the proposed method uses weak augmentation to train with samples selected as clean and maximizes the consistency between the model predictions of the weakly and strongly augmented training samples classified as noisy, with

$\theta^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}}\mathsf{clean}(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \times \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \mathcal{A}_{W}}\left\lbrack \ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(a(\mathbf{x}))) \right\rbrack + \left( 1 - \mathsf{clean}(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \right) \times \ell\left( \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \mathcal{A}_{S}}\left\lbrack f_{\theta}(a(\mathbf{x})) \right\rbrack,\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \mathcal{A}_{W}}\left\lbrack f_{\theta}(a(\mathbf{x})) \right\rbrack \right).$

(4.100)

Another type of data augmentation explored for noisy-label learning is MixUp (Zhang et al., 2018) that trains on convex combinations of training samples and respective labels, such as

$(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = \mathsf{MixUp}(\mathbf{x}_{i},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{j},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{j})\text{,\ where}\mathbf{x} = \lambda\mathbf{x}_{i} + (1 - \lambda)\mathbf{x}_{j},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} = \lambda{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i} + (1 - \lambda){\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{j},$

(4.101)

and λ ∼ β(a, b) representing a sample from a beta distribution parameterized by a and b. Arazo et al. (2019) proposed the use of MixUp in noisy-label learning with the following robust per-sample loss correction approach:

$\ell(i,j) = - \lambda \times \left\lbrack {((1 - w_{i}) \times {\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i} + w_{i} \times f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i}))}^{\top}\log(h) \right\rbrack - (1 - \lambda) \times \left\lbrack {((1 - w_{j}) \times {\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{j} + w_{i} \times f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{j}))}^{\top}\log(h) \right\rbrack,$

(4.102)

where h = fθ(λ × xi + (1 − λ) × xj), and wi, wj ∈ [0, 1] denote the confidence in the ground-truth labels and network predictions estimated from an unsupervised noise model.

Data augmentation has become a standard training technique in noisy-label learning. Virtually all modern approaches rely on some sort of data augmentation, ranging from simple approaches, such as with the use of regular augmentations during training, to sophisticated methods, like the ones described in this section. Consequently, we expect that data augmentation will continue to be explored in future methods as an essential technique to address noisy-label learning.

Test time augmentation (TTA) is a common post-hoc (i.e., applied after the training process is finished) machine learning technique used to improve generalization and robustness of models during testing. The basic idea is run the trained model on several augmented test samples, modified by applying several data transformations, and then the final prediction is based on aggregating the results from each augmented data (Shanmugam et al., 2021; Smart and Carneiro, 2023). The data augmentations, particularly when applied to image samples, consist of: random rotations, translations, scaling, flips, and color distortions. The application of these data transformations to the test samples followed by the calculation of the predictions for each augmented version effectively produces an ensemble of predictions. In particular, given a test image x and a set of image transformations denoted by 𝒜, the TTA prediction is:

${\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}^{\ast} = \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \mathcal{A}}\left\lbrack f_{\theta^{\ast}}(a(\mathbf{x})) \right\rbrack.$

(4.103)

Although quite simple, TTA shows substantial improvements in noisy-label classification (Smart and Carneiro, 2023). One can argue that this will significantly increase testing time, but since the data augmentations are mutually independent, they can in principle be applied in parallel, which means that this will not increase testing time. This is a topic that deserves further research.

4.3.7 Pseudo-labeling

Pseudo-labeling is a data-processing technique that is usually integrated with other methods, such as semi-supervised learning in Section 4.4.4. It is derived from the bootstrapping method (Reed et al., 2014) that modifies the training label with

$\widehat{\mathbf{y}} = \beta \times \widetilde{\mathbf{y}} + (1 - \beta) \times f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}),$

(4.104)

where β ∈ [0, 1]. However, instead of indiscriminately changing the labels of all training samples, pseudo-labeling is more selective and modifies only the samples that are more likely to contain noisy labels. For instance, in (Zhang et al., 2021c; Smart and Carneiro, 2023), pseudo-labeling consists of updating the training sample $(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}$ with $(\mathbf{x},\widehat{\mathbf{y}})$, where $\widehat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathsf{OneHot}(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))$ if $\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} \neq \widehat{\mathbf{y}}$ and maxy ∈ 𝒴(fθy(x)) > τ(t), where τ(t) is the prediction confidence threshold at training epoch t.

Modern pseudo-labeling methods tend to sub-divide the training set even more (e.g., clean-label, closed-set label noise, and open-set label noise) and apply different strategies to each sub-set, such as shown in Fig. 4.29. In DSOS (Albert et al., 2022), which addresses open and closed-set label noise problems, the pseudo-labeling is achieved by the function

$h(\mathbf{x}_{i},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i},u_{i},v_{i},\theta) = \frac{\exp\left( \frac{v_{i} \times {\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i}}{\alpha} \right)}{\sum_{c = 1}^{|\mathcal{Y}|}\exp\left( \frac{v_{i} \times {\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i}(c)}{\alpha} \right)}$

(4.105)

with α ∈ [0, 1], vi ∈ [0, 1], ui ∈ {0, 1}, and

${\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i} = (1 - u_{i}) \times {\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i} + u_{i} \times f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i}).$

(4.106)

The optimization of DSOS (Albert et al., 2022) dynamically estimates {ui}i = 1|𝒟| and {vi}i = 1|𝒟|, such that for open-set samples (vi ≈ 0), the pseudo-label is a uniform distribution over the class labels, for closed-set label noise, the pseudo-label is the model prediction, and for clean-label samples, the pseudo-label is the original training label. JoSRC (Yao et al., 2021b) proposes a similar pseudo-labeling technique as DSOS (Albert et al., 2022).

4.4 Training algorithms

This is one of the most fertile areas of research to address noisy-label learning. We begin by discussing meta-learning methods (Ren et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020c; Zhang and Pfister, 2021; Xu et al., 2021; Shu et al., 2019; Hoang et al., 2022; Dehghani et al., 2017) that automatically learn to weight and re-label training samples. Next, we present self-supervised pre-training techniques (Zheltonozhskii et al., 2022), which are present in virtually all methods that produce state-of-the-art results in the main benchmarks. Then, we describe multi-model approaches that use more than one model to mitigate the confirmation bias risk (Jiang et al., 2017; Malach and Shalev-Shwartz, 2017; Han et al., 2018c; Yu et al., 2019a; Wei et al., 2020), which is the risk of models learning from mistaken re-labellings and selected samples. Semi-supervised learning (SSL) is then presented (Ding et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020a; Zhou et al., 2021), where the goal is to separate the training samples into a labeled set and an unlabeled set, and then to treat the problem as an SSL task. Next, we present probabilistic graphical model techniques that aim to provide insightful understanding about the process of generating noisy labels for training samples (Lawrence and Schölkopf, 2001; Xiao et al., 2015; Vahdat, 2017; Yao et al., 2021a; Garg et al., 2023; Bae et al., 2022). We conclude the section with another type of training algorithm that has not received much attention for noisy-label learning, which is active learning (Bouguelia et al., 2018; Bernhardt et al., 2022; Goh and Mueller, 2023). Training algorithm techniques have been studied intensively in the field, and the most competitive noisy-label learning methods usually employ one of the algorithms presented in this section.

4.4.1 Meta-learning

In noisy-label learning problems, meta-learning algorithms (Ren et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020c; Zhang and Pfister, 2021; Xu et al., 2021; Shu et al., 2019; Hoang et al., 2022; Dehghani et al., 2017) are typically defined by two important features: 1) a bi-level optimization, and 2) the presence of a meta-parameter that weights the training samples. The bi-level optimization contains two nested optimization problems. The outer (or upper) optimization maximizes the performance of the meta-learner on the training task using a validation set, while the inner (or lower) optimization maximizes the performance of the model on the training task using the training set. The usual goal of the meta-learner is to automatically weight the training samples to facilitate the optimization of the training task, which usually results in down-weighting noisy-label samples and up-weighting clean-label samples.

An early example of a meta-learning method Dehghani et al. (2017) is shown in Fig. 4.30. In (Dehghani et al., 2017), the model architecture has a representation learning network gϕ : 𝒳 → 𝒵 that extracts features z ∈ 𝒵 from data x ∈ 𝒳. It also has the target network, denoted by fθ : 𝒵 → Δ|𝒴| − 1, and the confidence classifier wγ : 𝒵 × 𝒴 → ℝ that returns the confidence of matching the data x ∈ 𝒳 and label y ∈ 𝒴. We also have a training set with noisy labels $\mathcal{D}_{t} = {\{{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}_{i}\}}_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}_{t}|}$ and a small validation set containing both noisy and clean labels, defined by $\mathcal{D}_{v} = {\{{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y})}_{i}\}}_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}_{v}|}$, where |𝒟v| <  < |𝒟t|. Training is achieved in two stages, where the first stage optimizes the confidence model as follows:

$\phi^{\ast},\gamma^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\phi,\gamma}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{v}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) \in \mathcal{D}_{v}}\ell(\mathsf{diff}(\mathbf{y},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}),w_{\gamma}(g_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}),\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})),$

(4.107)

where $\mathsf{diff}(\mathbf{y},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})$ computes the difference between true label y and noisy label $\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}$. The second training stage then optimizes the target network as follows:

$\phi^{\ast},\theta^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\phi,\gamma}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{t}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}_{t}}w_{\gamma^{\ast}}(g_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}),\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \times \ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(g_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}))).$

(4.108)

The trained target network is then using to label test data. This work was followed by more sophisticated meta-learning approaches described below.

Arguably the most representative meta-learning method for noisy-label learning is the learning to re-weight (L2R) by Ren et al. (2018). L2R divides the original training set containing noisy labels, denoted by 𝒟, into mutually exclusive training and a validation sets 𝒟t and 𝒟v, respectively, where 𝒟t⋃𝒟v = 𝒟 and the labels of 𝒟v are guaranteed to be clean. L2R uses 𝒟v to learn a meta-parameter w ∈ Δ|𝒟t| − 1 which weights the loss ℓ(.) for each training sample in 𝒟t, similarly to the loss re-weighting technique in Section 4.2.3. This training sample weighting follows many utility criteria, such as informativeness, class-balanced distribution, and label cleanliness (Ren et al., 2018; Hoang et al., 2022). The meta-learning optimization is defined as:

$\mathbf{w}^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\mathbf{w} \in \Delta^{|\mathcal{D}_{t}| - 1}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{v}|}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}_{v}|}\ell(\mathbf{y}_{j},f_{\theta^{\ast}(\mathbf{w})}(\mathbf{x}_{j}))\text{s.t.:~}\theta^{\ast}(\mathbf{w}) = \arg\min\limits_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{t}|}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}_{t}|}\mathbf{w}_{i} \times \ell\left( {\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i}) \right),$

(4.109)

where the label yj from 𝒟v is assumed to be clean. In (4.109), the inner (lower) optimization trains the model fθ(.) using a weighted loss on the training set 𝒟t, while the outer (upper) optimization trains the meta-parameter w ∈ Δ|𝒟t| − 1 that weights the training set losses in the inner level.

The optimization in (4.109) is performed iteratively with the inner and outer stages. The inner stage is based on a one-step-ahead model parameter estimation to produce θ*(w) using the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on the training subset 𝒟t, defined by:

$\theta^{\ast}(\mathbf{w}) \approx \theta - \eta_{\theta}\nabla_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{t}|}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}_{t}|}\mathbf{w}_{i} \times \ell\left( {\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i}) \right),$

(4.110)

where ηθ is the learning rate. The outer stage consists of updating the meta-parameter w with a one SGD step on the loss computed from the validation set 𝒟v using the model's parameter θ*(ω) from (4.110), as in

$\mathbf{w}^{\ast} \approx \mathbf{w} - \eta_{\mathbf{w}}\nabla_{\mathbf{w}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{v}|}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}_{v}|}\ell\left( \mathbf{y}_{j},f_{\theta^{\ast}(\omega)}(\mathbf{x}_{j}) \right),$

(4.111)

where ηw represents the step size to update w. The learned meta-parameter w* is then projected to the probability simplex Δ|𝒟t| − 1 before it is used to train the model in (4.109).

Ren et al. (2018) analyze the optimization in (4.109) and formulate the following expression on the weighting of each training sample loss:

$\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{v}|}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}_{v}|}\left. \left\lbrack \frac{\partial}{\partial\mathbf{w}_{i}}\ell\left( \mathbf{y}_{j},f_{\theta^{\ast}(\omega,\lambda)}(\mathbf{x}_{j}) \right) \right\rbrack \right|_{\mathbf{w}_{i} = 0}\quad \propto - \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{v}|}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}_{v}|}\left\lbrack \sum\limits_{l = 1}^{L}({\mathbf{z}_{j,l - 1}^{(v)}}^{\top}\mathbf{z}_{i,l - 1}^{(t)})({\mathbf{g}_{j,l}^{(v)}}^{\top}\mathbf{g}_{i,l}^{(t)}) \right\rbrack,$

(4.112)

where zj, l − 1(v) denotes the feature produced by model layer l for validation sample xj, zi, l − 1(t) represents the lth-layer feature from the model for training sample xi, gj, l(v) is the lth-layer gradient for validation data xj, and gi, l(t) denotes the feature produced by model layer l for training data xi. Therefore, the loss reweighting factor wi for training sample xi is high if its feature and gradient are similar to at least one of the validation samples' feature and gradient; otherwise, wi is low.

A similar approach to L2R above is the Meta-weight-net (MWN) (Shu et al., 2019) that introduces a sample weighting model parameterized by ϕ ∈ Φ and represented with wϕ(.) that receives a loss value and returns a sample weight. The optimization is formulated as (see Fig. 4.31):

$\phi^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\phi}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{v}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) \in \mathcal{D}_{v}}\ell(\mathbf{y},f_{\theta_{\phi}^{\ast}}(\mathbf{x}))\text{s.t.:~}\theta_{\phi}^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{t}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}_{t}}w_{\phi}(\ell\left( \widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \right)) \times \ell\left( \widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \right).$

(4.113)

This algorithm runs in three iterative steps. Assuming the current training epoch represented by t, MWN first updates θ̂ϕ(t) with

${\widehat{\theta}}_{\phi}(t) \approx \theta(t) - \eta_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{t}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}_{t}}w_{\phi}\left( \ell\left( \widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta(t)}(\mathbf{x}) \right) \right)\nabla_{\theta}\ell\left( \widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \right)|_{\theta(t)},$

(4.114)

where ηθ represents the learning rate, and θ(t) denotes the model parameters at training iteration t. Then the parameter ϕ of the sample weighting model wϕ(.) is updated with:

$\phi(t + 1) \approx \phi(t) - \eta_{\phi}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{v}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) \in \mathcal{D}_{v}}\nabla_{\phi}\ell(\mathbf{y},f_{{\widehat{\theta}}_{\phi}(t)}(\mathbf{x}))|_{\phi(t)},$

(4.115)

where ηϕ represents the learning rate, and ϕ(t) is the sample weighting model's parameter at training iteration t. The last step consists of updating the model parameters with

$\theta(t + 1) \approx \theta(t) - \eta_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{t}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}_{t}}w_{\phi(t + 1)}\left( \ell\left( \widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta(t)}(\mathbf{x}) \right) \right)\nabla_{\theta}\ell\left( \widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \right)|_{\theta(t)}.$

(4.116)

The L2R approach is extended by Zhang et al. (2020c) with the introduction of a second meta-parameter βi ∈ [0, 1], i ∈ {1, …, |𝒟t|} that provides a re-labeling similar to the technique presented in Section 4.2.4. The re-labeling of training sample i is provided by

${\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i}(\beta_{i}) = \beta_{i} \times {\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i} + (1 - \beta_{i}) \times f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i}),$

(4.117)

which is a convex combination between the original training label and label produced by the model. The optimization in (4.109) is then reformulated as follows:

$\mathbf{w}^{\ast},\beta^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\mathbf{w},\beta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{v}|}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}_{v}|}\ell\left( \mathbf{y}_{j},f_{\theta^{\ast}{(\mathbf{w},\beta)}}(\mathbf{x}_{j}) \right)\text{s.t.:~}\theta^{\ast}(\mathbf{w},\beta) = \arg\min\limits_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{t}|}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}_{t}|}\mathbf{w}_{i} \times \ell\left( \widehat{\mathbf{y}}(\beta_{i}),f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i}) \right).$

(4.118)

The meta-parameter w is optimized as explained in (4.111), but β is updated as follows:

$\beta_{i}^{\ast} = \left\lbrack {sign}\left( - \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{v}|}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}_{v}|}\left\lbrack \frac{\partial}{\partial\beta_{i}}\ell\left( \mathbf{y}_{j},f_{\theta^{\ast}(\mathbf{w},\beta)}(\mathbf{x}_{j}) \right) \right\rbrack \right) \right\rbrack_{+},$

(4.119)

with [.]+ representing the rectification operator. The loss function proposed by Zhang et al. (2020c) is defined as:

$\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^{\ast} \times \ell\left( \widehat{\mathbf{y}}(\beta_{0}),f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \right) + \frac{\ell\left( \mathbf{y}^{\ast}(\beta^{\ast}),f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \right)}{B}\quad + \rho \times \ell\left( \mathbf{y}^{\gamma},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{\gamma}) \right) + \kappa \times {KL}\left\lbrack f_{\theta}\left( \mathbf{x} \right)||f_{\theta}\left( \widehat{\mathbf{x}} \right) \right\rbrack,$

(4.120)

where $\widehat{\mathbf{y}}(.)$ is the re-labeling defined in (4.117), β0 = 0.9, B is the batch size,

$\mathbf{y}^{\ast}(\beta^{\ast}) = \begin{cases} \widetilde{\mathbf{y}} & {\text{if~}\beta^{\ast} > 0,} \\ {f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})} & {\text{otherwise},} \\ \end{cases}$

yγ and xγ are calculated from the mixup operator (Zhang et al., 2018) using the training and validation sets, KL[.||.] represents the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, $\widehat{\mathbf{x}}$ is an augmented sample of x, and ρ and κ denote hyper-parameters.

All meta-learning methods above require a clean-label validation set 𝒟v, which is problematic to acquire, particularly in problems with many classes. Zhang and Pfister (2021) address this problem by replacing the clean-label dataset by a pseudo-clean validation set automatically built with a pusher function uθ : 𝒳 × 𝒴 → ℝ, as in:

$\mathcal{D}_{v}^{\ast} = \arg\max\limits_{\mathcal{D}_{v} \in \mathcal{D}}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}_{v}}u_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}),$

(4.121)

where $u_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = \ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta(t)}(\mathbf{x})) - \ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta(t + 1)}(\mathbf{x}))$. The maximization in (4.121) selects validation samples with the largest drops in losses between the models trained in steps t and t + 1, representing unstable samples that the model has started to fit, and leaves behind samples with continuous high or low losses because they are too hard or too easy to fit. Xu et al. (2021) propose a way to automatically detect a clean-label validation set by exploring the small-loss hypothesis with a Gaussian mixture model (GMM), similar to the approach in (4.24). Hoang et al. (2022) introduce a method to automatically select a clean-label validation set that has high-utility samples according to samples that maximize the gradient in (4.112).

Meta-learning methods provide a sound theoretical framework for the development of noisy-label learning methods since it automatically learns how to weight or re-label training samples to better optimize the target model. Nevertheless, such nice property comes with a relatively high computational cost since training takes 2 to 3 times longer compared with non meta-learning approaches, as can be seen from the 3-stage training in (4.114), (4.115), and (4.116), with each stage involving one-step SGD and the training of ϕ(t + 1) containing a second-order backpropagation. Additionally, the need for a clean (and balanced) validation set is a shortcoming that has recently been addressed (Zhang and Pfister, 2021; Xu et al., 2021; Hoang et al., 2022) with the caveat that the samples in this clean-label validation set may not actually be clean and may not be highly informative for the training process since these clean-label samples are likely to be the easy (or non-informative) samples to fit.

4.4.2 Self-supervised pre-training

Pre-training is a well-known technique to provide a strong initialization for a model by training it on a large amount of data using a general objective function to build effective representations of the training data (Erhan et al., 2010). These models can be trained using an external dataset (Krizhevsky et al., 2012), such as ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009), or they can rely on self-supervision (Noroozi and Favaro, 2016; Chen et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020). Self-supervised pre-training trains a model on a large amount of unlabeled data using a pretext task that does not require any labels. As shown in Fig. 4.32, examples of pretext tasks are the prediction of an image transformation (Gidaris et al., 2018; Novotny et al., 2018), or the contrastive learning based on the maximization of the similarity of the representations obtained from two views of the same training image and the minimization of the similarity between the representations from different training images (Chen et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020).

The use of ImageNet pre-trained models in noisy-label learning methods is quite common (Li et al., 2020a), but more recently, sophisticated self-supervised pre-training techniques were explored with outstanding results (Zheltonozhskii et al., 2022). In contrast to divide (C2D), Zheltonozhskii et al. (2022) define the “warm-up obstacle” as the inability of early-stopping discriminative learning processes to produce effective model initialization that can prevent the overfitting of noisy-label training samples. Zheltonozhskii et al. (2022) also observed that ImageNet pre-training is not only impractical, given the difficulty in finding relevant large-scale training sets that can be helpful for certain applications, but it can also be detrimental in some cases. C2D consists of simply pre-training the noisy-label learning model with the contrastive learning pre-training method SimCLR (Chen et al., 2020a), and then train the model with a state-of-the-art noisy-label learning method (Li et al., 2020a; Liu et al., 2020).

Self-supervised pre-training has become a model initialization technique present in virtually all state-of-the-art approaches that we will study in Chapter 5. In fact, methods that do not rely on self-supervised pre-training are unlikely to produce competitive results in the main benchmarks in the field. Nevertheless, it is unlikely that new self-supervised pre-training methods will be proposed in noisy-label learning literature. Instead, what is usually seen in noisy-label learning is the utilization of self-supervised pre-training techniques developed for general downstream tasks.

4.4.3 Multi-model training

The use of multiple models in noisy-label learning is a dominant technique usually designed to work together with sample selection to mitigate an issue widely known as confirmation bias. In this issue, a noisy-label sample may be classified as clean, which encourages the model to overfit such noisy-label sample, so it is again classified as clean in the next training iteration. This issue is mitigated by the training of multiple models because of the difficulty that multiple models will overfit the same noisy-label samples at the same training epoch, as shown in Fig. 4.33.

Decouple (Malach and Shalev-Shwartz, 2017) is a pioneer multi-model training approach for noisy-label learning, where two networks fθ1 : 𝒳 → Δ|𝒴| − 1 and fθ2 : 𝒳 → Δ|𝒴| − 1 are trained only on the training samples that they disagree, with

$\theta_{1}^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta_{1}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{S}}\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x}))\theta_{2}^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta_{2}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{S}}\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta_{2}}(\mathbf{x}))\text{s.t.~}\mathcal{S} = \left\{ (\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})|(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D},f_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x}) \neq f_{\theta_{2}}(\mathbf{x}) \right\}.$

(4.122)

The issue with decouple (Malach and Shalev-Shwartz, 2017) was that the disagreement set 𝒮 in (4.122) could contain many noisy-label samples that can lead to overfitting and confirmation bias.

The multi-model in (Jiang et al., 2017) relies on a collaborative learning of two models, the MentorNet and the StudentNet, with the StudentNet optimizing a loss re-weighted function, where the sample weights are dynamically estimated by the MentorNet with a data-driven curriculum using the features from the StudentNet. The MentorNet, denoted by the model gϕ(.) parameterized by ϕ ∈ Φ, provides a data-driven curriculum learning to train the StudentNet. The MentorNet model is trained as follows:

${\phi^{\ast},\theta^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\phi,\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}g_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{i}) \times \ell({\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i})) + G(g_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{i});\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}) + \gamma\ \times |\theta\|}_{2}^{2},$

(4.123)

where λ1, λ2 are regularization parameters for the penalization function G(wi; λ1, λ2) = 0.5λ22wi − (λ1 + λ2)wi, and zi = h(xi, yi, θ) is a feature comprising the loss, loss difference to the moving average, label and epoch percentage. In (4.123), the first term denotes the curriculum-weighted loss, while the second term specifies the curriculum, defined by a sequence of samples and respective weights for training the StudentNet. The optimization of (4.123) leads to the following closed-form solution:

$g_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{i}) = \begin{cases} {\delta(\ell_{i} \leq \lambda_{1}),} & {\text{~if~}\lambda_{2} = 0} \\ {\min\left( \max\left( 0,1 - \frac{\ell_{i} - \lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{2}} \right),1 \right),} & {\text{~if~}\lambda_{2} \neq 0} \\ \end{cases},$

(4.124)

where $\ell_{i} = \ell({\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i}))$, and δ(.) represents an indicator function. Hence, when λ2 = 0, we have a self-paced curriculum learning (Kumar et al., 2010), where the StudentNet is trained only with small-loss samples (i.e., samples with ℓi ≤ λ1 will have gϕ*(zi) = 1). On the other hand, when λ2 ≠ 0, the StudentNet is not trained with large-loss samples where ℓi ≥ λ2 + λ1, but it will be trained with samples weighted linearly by $1 - \frac{\ell_{i} - \lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{2}}$. Hence, similarly to (Kumar et al., 2010), λ1 and λ2 control the learning pace. Also, similarly to the decouple method presented before in (4.122), if the MentorNet mistakenly weights up a noisy-label sample, confirmation bias will follow.

These issues motivated the development of co-teaching (Han et al., 2018c) that explores the small-loss hypothesis (Arpit et al., 2017) in a multi-model scenario. Motivated by co-training (Blum and Mitchell, 1998), co-teaching has two models that will continuously select small-loss samples to train the peer model, as follows:

$\theta_{1}^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta_{1}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_{2}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{S}_{2}}\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x}))\theta_{2}^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta_{2}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_{1}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{S}_{1}}\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta_{2}}(\mathbf{x}))\text{s.t.~}\mathcal{S}_{1} = \left\{ (\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})|(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D},\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x})) < \tau) \right\},\mathcal{S}_{2} = \left\{ (\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})|(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D},\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta_{2}}(\mathbf{x})) < \tau) \right\},$

(4.125)

where τ varies during the training. The two models in (4.125) filter different types of label noise, which makes it difficult that both models will overfit the same noisy-label samples. Furthermore, even though one model can give noisy-label samples to the peer model, the robustness of both models to noisy-label samples from the early learning stages (Arpit et al., 2017) will mitigate the overfit to these noisy-label samples. We show an example of co-teaching in Fig. 4.34. Nevertheless, the two models in co-teaching soon reach a consensus during training, which means that both models become too similar, leading to a self-training strategy that becomes vulnerable to confirmation bias. Such issue can be mitigated with the decouple strategy (Malach and Shalev-Shwartz, 2017), described in (4.122), which can slow down the convergence rate of the co-teaching models. This led to the development of co-teaching+ (Yu et al., 2019a), which updates the models using small-loss samples with prediction disagreement between the classifiers, with:

$\theta_{1}^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta_{1}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_{2}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{S}_{2}}\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x}))\theta_{2}^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta_{2}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_{1}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{S}_{1}}\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta_{2}}(\mathbf{x}))\text{s.t.~}\mathcal{S} = \left\{ (\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})|(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D},f_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x}) \neq f_{\theta_{2}}(\mathbf{x}) \right\},\mathcal{S}_{1} = \left\{ (\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})|(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{S},\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x})) < \tau) \right\},\mathcal{S}_{2} = \left\{ (\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})|(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{S},\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta_{2}}(\mathbf{x})) < \tau) \right\}.$

(4.126)

Unfortunately, the combined constraints of small-loss and prediction disagreement in co-teaching+ (Yu et al., 2019a) can severely reduce the size of 𝒮1 and 𝒮2 in (4.126), particularly when the noise rate in 𝒟 is too high. Such inefficient use of the training set can damage the training process, which motivated Wei et al. (2020) to develop Joint Training with Co-Regularization (JoCoR). JoCor moves away from the maximization of the prediction disagreement to the maximization of the prediction agreement between the two classifiers fθ1(.) and fθ2(.) using a joint training loss for the two models and a regularization that replaces the sampling proposed in (Han et al., 2018c). This joint loss is also used to select the small-loss samples, which complicates the selection of noisy-label samples since they will need to have a small loss in both models to be selected. JoCor (Wei et al., 2020) optimizes the following loss function:

$\theta_{1}^{\ast},\theta_{2}^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta_{1},\theta_{2}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{S}}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\theta_{1},\theta_{2})\text{s.t.~}\mathcal{S} = \left\{ (\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})|(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D},\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\theta_{1},\theta_{2}) < \tau) \right\},$

(4.127)

where

$\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\theta_{1},\theta_{2}) = (1 - \lambda) \times \left( \ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x})) + \ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta_{2}}(\mathbf{x})) \right) + \lambda \times \left( \mathsf{KL}\lbrack f_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x})\| f_{\theta_{2}}(\mathbf{x})\rbrack + \mathsf{KL}\lbrack f_{\theta_{2}}(\mathbf{x})\| f_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x})\rbrack \right),$

(4.128)

with λ ∈ [0, 1] and KL[.] representing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence.

The use of the mean teacher model (Tarvainen and Valpola, 2017) that relies on a temporal ensembling of models, combined with the soft re-labeling of training samples based on a temporal ensembling of label and predictions are the two techniques explored by the self-ensemble label filtering (SELF) method (Nguyen et al., 2019). SELF filters out noisy-label samples by maintaining a temporal ensembling of predictions with ${\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{(t + 1)} = \alpha \times {\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{(t)} + (1 - \alpha) \times f_{\theta}(\mathbf{y})$, where ${\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{(0)} = 0$ and ${\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{(t)}$ represents the prediction ensemble at training iteration t. Then, training samples where $\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} \neq \mathsf{OneHot}({\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{(t + 1)})$ have their labels erased (i.e., they become un-labeled). Given these un-labeled and the remaining labeled training samples, SELF trains the mean-teacher model (Tarvainen and Valpola, 2017), which is a semi-supervised teacher-student learning model that outputs fθ(.). This model consists of the best teacher model, represented by the training epoch that provided the best accuracy in the validation set.

Multi-model training is one of the best tools developed to mitigate the confirmation bias problem, typically found in noisy-label learning methods. However, the need for training two separate models is generally seen as problematic given the larger run-time and memory complexity compared with other approaches based on a single model.

4.4.4 Semi-supervised learning

The experimental setup of semi-supervised learning (SSL) and noisy-label learning have one important commonality, which is that part of the dataset cannot be used for fully-supervised training. While in SSL, a subset of the training samples does not have labels, in noisy-label learning, a subset of the training set has wrong labels. The major difference between SSL and noisy-label learning is that the un-labeled samples in SSL are clearly marked, but we do not have clear demarcation of the training samples that carry a noisy label. Therefore, if sample selection techniques work effectively, then we can simply keep the labels of the samples classified as clean, and remove the labels from the training samples classified as noisy, and apply one of the SSL techniques. There are two challenges in noisy-label SSL methods, namely: it is inevitable that the training samples classified as clean will contain a small subset of noisy-label samples, and the samples classified as noisy may just be the clean-label informative samples that are quite important for the training process. Hence, much of the work in the application of SSL in noisy-label learning focus on addressing these two challenges.

There are three assumptions explored by the SSL approaches (Van Engelen and Hoos, 2020) that are useful in noisy-label learning: 1) images with neighboring representations in the feature space have similar labels; 2) decision boundary passes through low-density areas of the feature space; and 3) representations sharing a low-dimensional manifold in the feature space also share the same label. The main techniques explored by SSL approaches are the pseudo-labeling (Berthelot et al., 2019; Sohn et al., 2020; Arazo et al., 2020) (such as the ones presented in Section 4.3.7) and consistency learning (Laine and Aila, 2016; Tarvainen and Valpola, 2017; Polyak and Juditsky, 1992). Pseudo-labeling methods work by progressively annotating part of the un-labeled dataset, while consistency-based approaches minimize prediction discrepancies produced by the model using different input views obtained, for example, from data perturbations produced by augmentation functions. It has been noted that consistency-learning approaches tend to outperform pseudo-labeling methods, most likely because pseudo-labeling methods disregard part of the training set during optimization (Liu et al., 2022d). In fact, SSL approaches applied to noisy-label learning are mostly based on consistency-learning techniques, as we present below.

The first method to use SSL for noisy-label learning was the one proposed by (Ding et al., 2018), which explored consistency learning with the loss (see Fig. 4.35):

$\theta^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{c}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}_{c}}\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})) + \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}}{\| f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) - f_{\widehat{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})\|}_{2}^{2},$

(4.129)

where $\mathcal{D}_{c} = \{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})|(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D},\delta(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} = \mathsf{OneHot}(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))) = 1,f_{\theta}^{(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}(\mathbf{x}) > \tau\}$ denotes the set of pseudo-clean label samples, fθ̂(x) represents the model prediction after being perturbed with dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014), and the second loss maximizes the consistency between the prediction outputs after dropout perturbation applied to the model. We show the result produced by this model in Fig. 4.36. The approach proposed by Kong et al. (2019) explored the SSL assumption about the decision boundary passing through low-density areas of the feature space, with the following loss:

$\theta^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{c}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}_{c}}\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})) + \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{n}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}_{n}}\mathbb{H}_{r}(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}),\alpha),$

(4.130)

where 𝒟c is the set of pseudo-clean samples as defined in (4.64), 𝒟n = 𝒟 ∖ 𝒟c, and ℍr(fθ(x), α) denotes the Renyi entropy, defined by

$\mathbb{H}_{r}(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}),\alpha) = \frac{1}{1 - \alpha}\log\left( \sum\limits_{\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{Y}}\left( f_{\theta}^{(\mathbf{y})}(\mathbf{x}) \right)^{\alpha} \right),$

(4.131)

with α > 0, α ≠ 1.

As already explained in Section 4.4.3, the use of the mean teacher model (Tarvainen and Valpola, 2017) that relies on a temporal ensembling of models, combined with the soft re-labeling of training samples based on a temporal ensembling of predictions are the two techniques explored by the self-ensemble label filtering (SELF) method (Nguyen et al., 2019). SELF has the student and teacher models respectively denoted by fθ : 𝒳 × ℝ → Δ|𝒴| − 1 and fθ̂ : 𝒳 × ℝ → Δ|𝒴| − 1, where the student is optimized with

$\theta^{(t)} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{c}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}_{c}}\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\eta)) + \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}}{\| f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\eta) - f_{{\widehat{\theta}}^{(t - 1)}}(\mathbf{x},\widehat{\eta})\|}_{2}^{2},$

(4.132)

where η, η̂ ∈ ℝ denote noise variables (e.g., noise to the inputs or noise applied to the model), and t denotes the training epoch. The teacher is trained by ensembling its previous model with the student model from epoch t, as follows:

θ̂(t) = α × θ̂(t − 1) + (1 − α) × θ(t).

(4.133)

SELF selects the samples to be inserted into 𝒟c in (4.132) by maintaining a temporal ensembling of predictions with ${\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{(t)} = \alpha \times {\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{(t - 1)} + (1 - \alpha) \times f_{\widehat{\theta}}(\mathbf{x},0)$, where ${\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i}^{(0)} = 0$ and ${\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}_{i}^{(t)}$ represents the prediction ensemble at training epoch t. Then, training samples where $\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} = \mathsf{OneHot}({\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}^{(t + 1)})$ are inserted into 𝒟c. SELF also uses a noisy-label validation set to select the highest accuracy teacher model during the training process.

The application of the data augmentation technique MixUp (Zhang et al., 2018), defined in (4.101), into semi-supervised learning produced the MixMatch approach (Berthelot et al., 2019). MixMatch combines consistency learning and pseudo-labeling techniques and it was applied in noisy-label learning by the influential DivideMix method (Li et al., 2020a). MixMatch takes as input, a labeled and an un-labeled set. The labeled set is represented by training samples classified as clean-label and denoted by $\mathcal{D}_{c} = \{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})|(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D},\mathsf{clean}(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = 1\}$, and the un-labeled set, represented by training samples classified as noisy-label and denoted by $\mathcal{D}_{n} = \{(\mathbf{x})|(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D},\mathsf{clean}(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = 0\}$. Then, two sets of data augmented samples are built with

${\widehat{\mathcal{D}}}_{c} = \left\{ (\widehat{\mathbf{x}},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})|\widehat{\mathbf{x}} = a(\mathbf{x}),a \sim \mathcal{A},(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}_{c} \right\},{\widehat{\mathcal{D}}}_{n} = \left\{ (\widehat{\mathbf{x}},\mathbf{q})|\mathbf{q} = \mathsf{sharpen}\left( \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \mathcal{A}}\left\lbrack f_{\theta}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}}) \right\rbrack \right),\widehat{\mathbf{x}} = a(\mathbf{x}),a \sim \mathcal{A},\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{D}_{n} \right\},$

(4.134)

where 𝒜 is a set of random horizontal flips and crops augmentation functions, denoted by a : 𝒳 → 𝒳, and sharpen : Δ|𝒴| − 1 → Δ|𝒴| − 1 denotes a function to sharpen the categorical distribution by adjusting the distribution's temperature. The next stage of MixMatch relies on augmenting the data from ${\widehat{\mathcal{D}}}_{c}$ and ${\widehat{\mathcal{D}}}_{n}$ with MixUp (Zhang et al., 2018) defined in (4.101), as

$\mathcal{D}_{c}^{\prime} = \left\{ (\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})|(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = \mathsf{MixUp}(\mathbf{x}_{i},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{j},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{j}),(\mathbf{x}_{i},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i}) \in {\widehat{\mathcal{D}}}_{c},(\mathbf{x}_{j},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{j}) \in \mathcal{W} \right\},\mathcal{D}_{n}^{\prime} = \left\{ (\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})|(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = \mathsf{MixUp}(\mathbf{x}_{i},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{j},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{j}),(\mathbf{x}_{i},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i}) \in {\widehat{\mathcal{D}}}_{n},(\mathbf{x}_{j},{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{j}) \in \mathcal{W} \right\},$

(4.135)

where $\mathcal{W} = \mathsf{shuffle}({\widehat{\mathcal{D}}}_{c}\bigcup{\widehat{\mathcal{D}}}_{n})$ is a set containing the shuffled contents of the union between the labeled and unlabeled sets from (4.134). The last step in MixMatch consists of the following optimization using the sets built in (4.135):

${\theta^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{c}^{\prime}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}_{c}^{\prime}}\ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})) + \frac{\lambda_{n}}{|\mathcal{Y}| \times |\mathcal{D}_{n}^{\prime}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}_{n}^{\prime}}\|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} - f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\|}_{2}^{2},$

(4.136)

where λU weights the loss from the un-labeled set.

Another type of SSL based on consistency loss for noisy-label learning is the RoCL (Zhou et al., 2021), introduced in Section 4.3.2. Essentially, the first stage of RoCL consists of a supervised learning from pseudo-clean samples, which is followed by a second stage represented by SSL on pseudo-labeled noisy samples produced by a time-ensemble of the model and data augmentations. The optimization of RoCL is defined by

$\theta^{(t + 1)} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta}\left( \frac{\lambda}{\tau_{1}} \right) \times \log\left( \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{c}|}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}_{c}|}\exp\left( \tau_{1}\ell({\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}}_{i},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i})) \right) \right) + \left( \frac{1 - \lambda}{\tau_{2}} \right) \times \log\left( \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{c}|}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}_{c}|}\exp\left( \tau_{2} \times \zeta_{i}^{(t)} \right) \right),$

(4.137)

where 𝒟c is the dataset containing pseudo-clean samples defined in (4.56), and ζi(t) is the instantaneous consistency loss defined in (4.55).

Some SSL methods developed for noisy-label learning are based on pseudo-labeling, as is the case with the modified co-teaching with self-supervision and re-labeling (mCT-S2R) (Mandal et al., 2020). The mCT-S2R approach extends co-teaching (Han et al., 2018c), presented in (4.125), by adding pseudo-labeling and re-training stages. The pseudo-labeling approach is done by selecting one of the models, say the one parameterized by θ1, and dividing the training set into samples with small loss 𝒟c with the remaining samples with large loss, forming the set 𝒟n = 𝒟 ∖ 𝒟c. Then, taking the features, denoted by z ∈ 𝒵, from an intermediate layer of fθ1(x), we form the set of small-loss features $\mathcal{Z}_{c} = \{(\mathbf{z},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})|\mathbf{z}\text{~extracted\ from~}f_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x}),(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}_{c}\}$, and the set of large-loss features $\mathcal{Z}_{n} = \{(\mathbf{z},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})|\mathbf{z}\text{~extracted\ from~}f_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x}),(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}_{n}\}$. Next, we compute the class-wise prototype vectors, computed with the mean vector {μy}y ∈ 𝒴 with $\mu_{\mathbf{y}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{(\mathbf{z},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{Z}_{c}}\delta(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{y}) \times \mathbf{z}$, where $N = \sum_{(\mathbf{z},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{Z}_{c}}\delta(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{y})$, and δ(.) is the indicator function. The new labels for the large-loss features are computed with:

$\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} = \mathsf{OneHot}\left( \mathsf{softmax}\left( \lbrack - d_{1},..., - d_{|\mathcal{Y}|}\rbrack \right) \right)$

(4.138)

if max (softmax([−d1,...,−d|𝒴|])) > κ, where dy = ∥z − μy∥22 represents the distance to the prototype of class y, softmax(.) returns a categorical distribution using the softmax activation, and OneHot(.) returns the one-hot vector from this categorical distribution. The last step consists of taking 𝒟c and the pseudo-labeled samples from 𝒟n to fine-tune the model fθ1(.). The pseudo-labeling approach above has two weaknesses: 1) it only uses a single prototype per class, which may not allow a reliable representation of the feature distribution for each class when it has multiple modes; and 2) its non-iterative nature may under-utilize the training set if part of it never gets pseudo-labeled. Both issues have been addressed by Han et al. (2019), who proposed the estimation of multiple prototypes to represent each class, where the re-labeling and training follows an iterative process. Another interesting point explored in (Han et al., 2019) is that the loss function is represented by a convex combination of the loss with the original label and a loss with the pseudo-label, as in:

$\theta^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{pl}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\widehat{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}_{pl}}\alpha \times \ell(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})) + (1 - \alpha) \times \ell(\widehat{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})),$

(4.139)

where α ∈ [0, 1] is close to 1 at the first training iterations and it decreases toward 0 as training progress, and $\widehat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the pseudo-label for the training sample stored in 𝒟pl that has both the original training label and the pseudo label.

Lately, the combination of pseudo-labeling and consistency learning has been explored in SSL methods for noisy label learning. The Sample Selection and Relabeling (SSR) approach (Feng et al., 2021), which has a sample selection technique discussed in Section 4.3.3 and a data cleaning method explained in Section 4.3.2, explores a consistency loss with

$\theta^{\ast} = \arg\min\limits_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{pl}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widehat{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}_{pl}}\ell(\widehat{\mathbf{y}},f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})) + \ell_{fc}(f_{\theta}(a_{1}(\mathbf{x})),f_{\theta}(a_{2}(\mathbf{x}))),$

(4.140)

where a1, a2 ∼ 𝒜 denote data augmentation functions sampled from a set of functions 𝒜, ℓfc(.) is a consistency loss represented by the cosine distance between two augmented views of the training data x, and $\widehat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the pseudo-label for training sample x obtained from the model if the confidence of the classifier in the pseudo-labeled class (i.e., $f_{\theta}^{(\widehat{\mathbf{y}})}(\mathbf{x})$) is above a certain threshold, otherwise, $\widehat{\mathbf{y}} = \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}$.

Semi-supervised learning is a technique that has been shown to produce outstanding results in noisy-label learning, particularly the methods based on consistency learning. The main issue with SSL-based approaches is the need to classify training samples into clean and noisy, which produces a non-negligible set of samples that are mistakenly classified as clean, but contain noisy labels, biasing the training process. It also mistakenly classifies hard clean-label samples as noisy-label ones, reducing the robustness of the classifier to those hard samples. Hence, much of the research in this area has focused on how to design the best possible classifier of clean and noisy-label samples.

4.4.5 Probabilistic graphical model

Probabilistic graphical models (PGM) have been used in the development of noisy-label learning methods even before deep learning started dominating the field (Krizhevsky et al., 2012). For example, the PGM introduced by Lawrence and Schölkopf (2001) for noisy-label learning using a kernel Fisher discriminant (KFD), was proposed with a random variable X representing the data, another random variable Ỹ denoting the noisy label, and a latent random variable Y representing the clean label, as shown in Fig. 4.37(a). The learning using such PGM is based on

$\theta^{\ast} = \arg\max\limits_{\theta}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}}\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}),$

(4.141)

where θ parameterizes the class conditional density, and

$\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = \sum\limits_{\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{Y}}q(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})\frac{q(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}{q(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})} = \sum\limits_{\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{Y}}q(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})\log\frac{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}\frac{q(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}{q(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})} = \sum\limits_{\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{Y}}q(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})\log\frac{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}{q(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})} + \sum\limits_{\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{Y}}q(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})\log\frac{q(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})} = \underset{\text{ELBO}}{\underset{︸}{\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}\left\lbrack \log\frac{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}{q(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})} \right\rbrack}} + \underset{\geq 0}{\underset{︸}{\mathsf{KL}\left\lbrack q(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})\| p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \right\rbrack}}.$

(4.142)

In (4.142), we have the evidence lower bound (ELBO) and the (non-negative term) Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the variational posterior $q(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})$ and the true posterior $p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})$. Note that variational posterior is designed to approximate the complex true posterior. The maximization in (4.141) relies on the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm (Dempster et al., 1977), where in the tth iteration, the E-step consists of computing the posterior distribution of Y with

$p_{\theta^{(t)}}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = \frac{p_{\theta^{(t)}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}{p_{\theta^{(t)}}(\mathbf{x}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})},$

(4.143)

followed by setting $q(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = p_{\theta^{(t)}}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})$ to make the KL divergence in (4.142) equal to zero. The M-step then maximizes the ELBO in (4.142) with respect to θ = {θ1, θ2}, by representing

$p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = p_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{y})p_{\theta_{2}}(\mathbf{y}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}),$

(4.144)

where pθ1(x|y) is modeled with a normal distribution, and $p_{\theta_{2}}(\mathbf{y}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})$ is a label transition modeled with a transition table. We show the functionality of this approach in Fig. 4.38.

The PGM in (Xiao et al., 2015) uses two latent variables, namely the clean label Y and the label noise type N, with the graph structure displayed in Fig. 4.37(b). The label noise type is a ternary random variable associated with the following semantic classes: 1) n = [1, 0, 0]: label is noise free, which implies that Y = Ỹ; 2) n = [0, 1, 0]: symmetric noise, where the label has random noise, so Ỹ can take any possible label, except Y; and 3) n = [0, 0, 1]: asymmetric noise, so Ỹ can take labels that are confusing with Y. Using the graph structure above, we can formulate the following decomposition:

$p(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{n}|\mathbf{x}) = p(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{y},\mathbf{n})p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{n}|\mathbf{x}),$

(4.145)

where

$p(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{y},\mathbf{n}) = \begin{cases} {\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}\mathbf{I}\mathbf{y},} & {\text{if~}\mathbf{n} = \lbrack 1,0,0\rbrack} \\ {\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}| - 1}\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{U} - \mathbf{I})\mathbf{y},} & {\text{if~}\mathbf{n} = \lbrack 0,1,0\rbrack} \\ {\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{y},} & {\text{if~}\mathbf{n} = \lbrack 0,0,1\rbrack} \\ \end{cases},$

(4.146)

where I represents the |𝒴| × |𝒴| identity matrix, U denotes the |𝒴| × |𝒴| matrix with all elements equal to one, C is a |𝒴| × |𝒴| sparse stochastic matrix with tr(C) = 0, and Cij represents the transition probability between classes i and j. The optimization maximizes the following log-likelihood

$\theta^{\ast} = \arg\max\limits_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}}\log p_{\theta}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{x}),$

(4.147)

where we introduce the variational posterior $q(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{n}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})$, with

$\begin{aligned} {\log p_{\theta}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{x})} & {= \underset{\text{ELBO}}{\underset{︸}{\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{n}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}\left\lbrack \log\frac{p_{\theta}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})}{q(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{n}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})} \right\rbrack}} + \underset{\geq 0}{\underset{︸}{\mathsf{KL}\left\lbrack q(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{n}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})||p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \right\rbrack}}} \\ \end{aligned},$

(4.148)

using the same derivation steps as in (4.142). This optimization is also based on the EM algorithm (Dempster et al., 1977), where in the E-step at the tth iteration, we set the KL divergence to zero, by setting $q(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{n}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = p_{\theta^{(t)}}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{n}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})$, where

$p_{\theta^{(t)}}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{n}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = \frac{p_{\theta^{(t)}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{n}|\mathbf{x})}{p_{\theta^{(t)}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{x})} = \frac{p_{\theta^{(t)}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{y},\mathbf{n})p_{\theta^{(t)}}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})p_{\theta^{(t)}}(\mathbf{n}|\mathbf{x})}{\sum_{\mathbf{y}^{\prime},\mathbf{n}^{\prime}}p_{\theta^{(t)}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{y}^{\prime},\mathbf{n}^{\prime})p_{\theta^{(t)}}(\mathbf{y}^{\prime}|\mathbf{x})p_{\theta^{(t)}}(\mathbf{n}^{\prime}|\mathbf{x})}.$

(4.149)

The M-step maximizes the ELBO in (4.148) with respect to θ = {θ1, θ2, θ3} that is a set of parameters for the models $p_{\theta_{1}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{y},\mathbf{n})$, pθ2(y|x), and pθ3(n|x). While pθ2(y|x) and pθ3(n|x) are modeled with deep learning models, $p_{\theta_{1}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{y},\mathbf{n})$ is a label transition model trained with a separate set of data containing clean and noisy labels with $\mathcal{D}_{c} = {\{{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}_{i}\}}_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{D}_{c}|}$.

A similar PGM has been proposed by Vahdat (2017) that relies on an undirected graphical model depicted in with the graph structure of Fig. 4.37(c), where Y represents the latent clean label random variable and H denotes the random binary variable in the space ℋ that models the correlations between labels. The model is estimated with the following optimization

$\theta^{\ast} = \arg\max\limits_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}}\log p_{\theta}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{x}) + \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{c}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}_{c}}\log p_{\theta}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}),$

(4.150)

where 𝒟 is the original training set with noisy labels and 𝒟c is a separate training set containing noisy and clean labels. The first term in (4.150) is decomposed as

$\log p_{\theta}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{x}) = \underset{\text{ELBO}}{\underset{︸}{\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}\left\lbrack \log\frac{p_{\theta}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h}|\mathbf{x})}{q(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})} \right\rbrack}} + \underset{\geq 0}{\underset{︸}{\mathsf{KL}\left\lbrack q(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})||p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \right\rbrack}},$

(4.151)

while the second term is decomposed as

$\log p_{\theta}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}) = \underset{\text{ELBO}}{\underset{︸}{\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{h}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}\left\lbrack \log\frac{p_{\theta}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h}|\mathbf{x})}{q(\mathbf{h}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})} \right\rbrack}} + \underset{\geq 0}{\underset{︸}{\mathsf{KL}\left\lbrack q(\mathbf{h}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})||p_{\theta}(\mathbf{h}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \right\rbrack}},$

(4.152)

where $q(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})$ is a variational posterior that approximates the true posterior $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})$, and $q(\mathbf{h}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})$ is another variational posterior to approximate the posterior $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{h}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})$. Vahdat (2017) mentions that these variational distributions can overfit the data, particularly at the beginning of the training, so a regularization based on auxiliary (e.g., non-image) sources of information to extract the relationship between noisy and clean labels is proposed. This auxiliary distribution is denoted by the joint probability of noisy and clean labels and hidden binary states $p_{aux}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h})$, which is modeled by restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM). The regularization for (4.151) is $\alpha \times \mathsf{KL}\left\lbrack q(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})||p_{aux}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \right\rbrack$, where α ≥ 0; and for (4.152) is $\alpha \times \mathsf{KL}\left\lbrack q(\mathbf{h}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})||p_{aux}(\mathbf{h}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \right\rbrack$, where α ≥ 0. Finally, the training is based on the EM algorithm (Dempster et al., 1977), where the E-step during the tth iteration sets

$q(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \propto \left\lbrack p_{\theta^{(t)}}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \times p_{aux}^{\alpha}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \right\rbrack^{\frac{1}{\alpha + 1}},$

(4.153)

and

$q(\mathbf{h}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \propto \left\lbrack p_{\theta^{(t)}}(\mathbf{h}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \times p_{aux}^{\alpha}(\mathbf{h}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \right\rbrack^{\frac{1}{\alpha + 1}}.$

(4.154)

The M-step maximizes the ELBO terms in (4.151) and (4.152) with respect to θ by fixing q(.) and following the direction of the gradients:

$\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}\left\lbrack \log p_{\theta}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h}|\mathbf{x}) \right\rbrack\text{~,and~}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{h}|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}\left\lbrack \log p_{\theta}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h}|\mathbf{x}) \right\rbrack,$

(4.155)

where

$p_{\theta}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h}|\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{Z_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}\exp\left( - \mathsf{E}_{\theta}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h},\mathbf{x}) \right),$

(4.156)

with θ representing the bias terms aϕ(x), bϕ(x), c and the matrix W denoting the pairwise interactions, as follows

$\mathsf{E}_{\theta}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h},\mathbf{x}) = - a_{\phi}{(\mathbf{x})}^{\top}\mathbf{y} - b_{\phi}{(\mathbf{x})}^{\top}\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{c}^{\top}\mathbf{h} - \mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{h}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}.$

(4.157)

Also in (4.156), the normalization is defined by

$Z_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum\limits_{\widetilde{\mathbf{y}} \in \mathcal{Y},\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{Y},\mathbf{h} \in \mathcal{H}}\exp\left( - \mathsf{E}_{\theta}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{h},\mathbf{x}) \right).$

(4.158)

The PGMs introduced in (Garg et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2021a) follow the model shown in Fig. 4.37(d), where Y is a latent clean random variable and Z is a latent image feature random variable. The optimization is performed by

$\theta^{\ast} = \arg\max\limits_{\theta}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum\limits_{(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in \mathcal{D}}\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}),$

(4.159)

where

$\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = \underset{\text{ELBO}}{\underset{︸}{\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}\left\lbrack \log\frac{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})}{q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})} \right\rbrack}} + \underset{\geq 0}{\underset{︸}{\mathsf{KL}\left\lbrack q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}})\| p_{\theta}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \right\rbrack}}.$

(4.160)

In (4.160), we have

$p_{\theta}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = p(\mathbf{y})p(\mathbf{z})p_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z})p_{\theta_{2}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x}),$

(4.161)

where p(z) is modeled by a multivariate normal distribution (zero mean, identity covariance), p(y) by a uniform distribution, and pθ1(.) and pθ2(.) are the decoders modeled by deep learning networks. Also in (4.160), we have

$q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) = q_{\phi_{1}}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})q_{\phi_{2}}(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x}),$

(4.162)

representing the encoders modeled by deep learning networks. The optimization in (4.159) consists of maximizing the ELBO, as follows:
